'''''Acer''''' is a [[genus]] of [[tree]]s and [[shrub]]s commonly known as '''maples'''. The [[genus]] is placed in the soapberry family [[Sapindaceae]].<ref name="Joyce-2023">{{cite journal | last1=Joyce | first1=Elizabeth M. | last2=Appelhans | first2=Marc S. | last3=Buerki | first3=Sven | last4=Cheek | first4=Martin | last5=de Vos | first5=Jurriaan M. | last6=Pirani | first6=José R. | last7=Zuntini | first7=Alexandre R. | last8=Bachelier | first8=Julien B. | last9=Bayly | first9=Michael J. | last10=Callmander | first10=Martin W. | last11=Devecchi | first11=Marcelo F. | last12=Pell | first12=Susan K. | last13=Groppo | first13=Milton | last14=Lowry | first14=Porter P. | last15=Mitchell | first15=John | last16=Siniscalchi | first16=Carolina M. | last17=Munzinger | first17=Jérôme | last18=Orel | first18=Harvey K. | last19=Pannell | first19=Caroline M. | last20=Nauheimer | first20=Lars | last21=Sauquet | first21=Hervé | last22=Weeks | first22=Andrea | last23=Muellner-Riehl | first23=Alexandra N. | last24=Leitch | first24=Ilia J. | last25=Maurin | first25=Olivier | last26=Forest | first26=Félix | last27=Nargar | first27=Katharina | last28=Thiele | first28=Kevin R. | last29=Baker | first29=William J. | last30=Crayn | first30=Darren M. | title=Phylogenomic analyses of Sapindales support new family relationships, rapid Mid-Cretaceous Hothouse diversification, and heterogeneous histories of gene duplication | journal=Frontiers in Plant Science | publisher=Frontiers Media SA | volume=14 | date=2023-03-07 | issn=1664-462X | doi=10.3389/fpls.2023.1063174 | doi-access=free | article-number=1063174 | pmid=36959945 | pmc=10028101 | bibcode=2023FrPS...1463174J }}</ref><ref name="Stevens-2001">Stevens, P. F. (2001 onwards). Angiosperm Phylogeny Website. Version 9, June 2008 [and more or less continuously updated since]. http://www.mobot.org/MOBOT/research/APweb/.</ref> There are approximately 132 [[species]], most of which are native to [[East Asia]],<ref>{{eFloras|2|100167|Acer|first1=Tingzhi|last1=Xu|first2=Yousheng|last2=Chen|first3=Piet C.|last3=de Jong|first4=Herman John|last4=Oterdoom|first5=Chin-Sung|last5=Chang|volume=11|access-date=27 May 2012}}</ref> with a number also appearing in [[Europe]], northern [[Africa]], and [[North America]]. Only one species, ''[[Acer laurinum]]'', extends to the [[Southern Hemisphere]].<ref name="Gibbs-2009">Gibbs, D. & Chen, Y. (2009) [http://www.bgci.org/files/Worldwide/News/sepdec09/maples_red_list.pdf The Red List of Maples] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190528200257/http://www.bgci.org/files/Worldwide/News/sepdec09/maples_red_list.pdf |date=2019-05-28 }} Botanic Gardens Conservation International (BGCI) {{ISBN|978-1-905164-31-8}}</ref> The [[type species]] of the genus is the sycamore maple ''[[Acer pseudoplatanus]]'', one of the most common maple species in Europe.<ref name="van Gelderen-1999">van Gelderen, C. J. & van Gelderen, D. M. (1999). ''[[iarchive:maplesforgardens0000geld/mode/2up|Maples for Gardens: A Color Encyclopedia]]'' {{ISBN|978-0-585-25457-9}} </ref> Most maples have easily identifiable [[palmate]] leaves (with a few exceptions, such as ''[[Acer carpinifolium]]'', ''[[Acer laurinum]]'', and ''[[Acer negundo]]'') and all share distinctive [[samara (fruit)|winged fruit]]s. The closest relative of the maples is the small east Asian genus ''[[Dipteronia]]'', followed by the more widespread genus ''[[Aesculus]]'' (buckeyes and horse-chestnuts).<ref name="Joyce-2023"/> [[Maple syrup]] is made from the sap of some maple species. It is one of the most common genera of trees in Asia. Many maple species are grown in gardens where they are valued for their autumn colour and often decorative foliage, some also for their attractive flowers, fruit, or bark.<ref name="Crowley-2020">[https://treesandshrubsonline.org/articles/acer/] Crowley (2020) Acer L. from the website Trees and Shrubs Online</ref>

==Evolutionary history==
[[File:Acer florissanti UCMP-3831 NPS img1.jpg|thumb|A leaf fossil of ''[[Acer florissanti]]'' from the Late Eocene in the [[Florissant Formation]], [[Florissant, Colorado|Florissant]], [[Colorado]], [[United States]]]]
The closest relative of ''Acer'' is ''[[Dipteronia]]'', which only has two living species in China, but has a fossil record extending back to the middle [[Paleocene]] in North America. The oldest known fossils of ''Acer'' are from the late Paleocene of [[Northeast Asia]] and northern North America, around 60 million years old. The oldest fossils of ''Acer'' in Europe are from [[Svalbard]], dating to the late [[Eocene]] ([[Priabonian]] ~38–34 million years ago).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Areces-Berazain |first1=Fabiola |last2=Hinsinger |first2=Damien D. |last3=Strijk |first3=Joeri S. |date=March 2021 |title=Genome-wide supermatrix analyses of maples (Acer, Sapindaceae) reveal recurring inter-continental migration, mass extinction, and rapid lineage divergence |journal=Genomics |language=en |volume=113 |issue=2 |pages=681–692 |doi=10.1016/j.ygeno.2021.01.014|pmid=33508445 |s2cid=231754169 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Morphology==
[[File:Acer saccharum.jpg|thumb|''[[Acer saccharum]]'' (sugar maple)]]
Most maples or acers are trees growing to a height of {{convert|10|-|45|m|abbr=on}}. Others are shrubs less than 10&nbsp;meters tall with a number of small [[trunk (botany)|trunks]] originating at about ground level. Most species are [[deciduous]], and many are renowned for their [[autumn leaf colour]]s, but a few in southern Asia and the [[Mediterranean region]] are mostly [[evergreen]]. Most are [[Shade tolerance|shade-tolerant]] when young and are often riparian, understory, or pioneer species rather than climax overstory trees. There are a few exceptions such as [[sugar maple]], which may form monodominant forests. Many of the [[root]] systems are typically dense and fibrous, inhibiting the growth of other vegetation underneath them. A few species, notably ''[[Acer cappadocicum]]'', frequently produce [[root sprout]]s, which can develop into [[clonal colony|clonal colonies]].<ref name="van Gelderen-1999"/>

[[File:Vine Maple leaves and flowers.jpg|thumb|''[[Acer circinatum]]'' (vine maple) leaves showing the palmate veining typical of most species]]
Maples are distinguished by opposite [[leaf]] arrangement. The leaves in most species are [[leaf shape|palmate]] veined and lobed, with 3 to 9 (rarely to 13) veins each leading to a lobe, one of which is central or apical. A small number of species differ in having palmate compound, [[leaf shape|pinnate]] compound, pinnate veined or unlobed leaves. Several species, including ''[[Acer griseum]]'' (paperbark maple), ''[[Acer mandshuricum]]'' (Manchurian maple), ''[[Acer maximowiczianum]]'' (Nikko maple) and ''[[Acer triflorum]]'' (three-flowered maple), have trifoliate leaves. One species, ''[[Acer negundo]]'' (box-elder or Manitoba maple), has pinnately compound leaves that may be simply trifoliate or may have five, seven, or rarely nine leaflets. A few, such as ''[[Acer laevigatum]]'' (Nepal maple) and ''[[Acer carpinifolium]]'' (hornbeam maple), have pinnately veined simple leaves.

Maple species, such as ''[[Acer rubrum]]'', may be [[monoecious]], [[dioecious]] or [[polygamodioecious]]. The [[flower]]s are regular, [[symmetry (biology)#Pentamerism|pentamerous]], and borne in [[raceme]]s, [[corymb]]s, or [[umbel]]s. They have four or five [[sepal]]s, four or five [[petal]]s about 1–6&nbsp;mm long (absent in some species), four to ten [[stamen]]s about 6–10&nbsp;mm long, and two [[pistil]]s or a pistil with two styles. The [[ovary (botany)|ovary]] is superior and has two [[carpel]]s, whose wings elongate the flowers, making it easy to tell which flowers are female. Maples flower in late [[winter]] or early [[spring (season)|spring]], in most species with or just after the appearance of the leaves, but in some before the trees leaf out.<ref name="Huxley-1992">Huxley, A., ed. (1992). ''New RHS Dictionary of Gardening''. Macmillan {{ISBN|0-333-47494-5}}.</ref>

Maple flowers are green, yellow, orange or red. Though individually small, the effect of an entire tree in flower can be striking in several species. Some maples are an early spring source of [[pollen]] and [[nectar]] for [[bee]]s.

[[File:3D rendering of a µCT scan of a maple seed.ogv|thumb|right|[[3D rendering]] of a [[Computed tomography|μCT]] scan of a samara. Resolution is about 45 μm/[[voxel]].]]
The distinctive [[fruit]]s are called [[samara (fruit)|samaras]], "maple keys", "helicopters", "whirlybirds" or "polynoses". These [[seed]]s occur in distinctive pairs each containing one seed enclosed in a "nutlet" attached to a flattened wing of fibrous, papery tissue. They are shaped to spin as they fall and to carry the seeds a considerable distance on the wind. People often call them "helicopters" due to the way that they spin as they fall. During World War II, the US Army developed a special airdrop supply carrier that could carry up to {{convert|65|lb}} of supplies and was based on the maple seed.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=gN8DAAAAMBAJ&dq=Popular+Mechanics+Science+installing+linoleum&pg=PA75 "Sky Hook Spirals from Plane"] ''Popular Mechanics'', December 1944, p. 75.</ref> Seed maturation is usually in a few weeks to six months after flowering, with [[Biological dispersal|seed dispersal]] shortly after maturity. However, one tree can release hundreds of thousands of seeds at a time. Depending on the species, the seeds can be small and green to orange and big with thicker seed pods. The green seeds are released in pairs, sometimes with the stems still connected. The yellow seeds are released individually and almost always without the stems. Most species require [[stratification (botany)|stratification]] in order to [[germination|germinate]], and some seeds can remain dormant in the soil for several years before germinating.<ref name="van Gelderen-1999"/>

The genus ''Acer'', together with genus ''Dipteronia'', were formerly often classified in a [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] of their own, the [[Aceraceae]], but recent botanical consensus, including the [[Angiosperm Phylogeny Group]] system, includes them in the family [[Sapindaceae]]; their exclusion from Sapindaceae would leave that family [[paraphyly|paraphyletic]]. Within Sapindaceae, ''Acer'' is placed in the [[subfamily]] [[Hippocastanoideae]].<ref name="Joyce-2023"/> The genus is subdivided by its morphology into a multitude of sections and subsections.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.inh.co.jp/~hayasida/Ebunrui1.html|title=Classification of Genus ''Acer''|date=12 August 2007|access-date=19 November 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070812014108/http://www.inh.co.jp/~hayasida/Ebunrui1.html|archive-date=12 August 2007}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Areces-Berazain|first1=Fabiola|last2=Wang|first2=Yixi|last3=Hinsinger|first3=Damien D.|last4=Strijk|first4=Joeri S.|date=2020-07-13|title=Plastome comparative genomics in maples resolves the infrageneric backbone relationships|journal=PeerJ|language=en|volume=8|article-number=e9483|doi=10.7717/peerj.9483|issn=2167-8359|pmc=7365138|pmid=32742784 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Molecular studies incorporating DNA sequence data from both chloroplast and nuclear genomes, aiming to resolve the internal relationships and reconstruct the evolutionary history of the group, suggest a Late Paleocene origin for the group, appearing first in the northeastern Palearctic. Rapid lineage divergence was followed by several independent dispersals to the Nearctic and Western Palearctic regions.<ref name="Renner-2008">{{Cite journal|last1=Renner|first1=Susanne S|last2=Grimm|first2=Guido W|last3=Schneeweiss|first3=Gerald M|last4=Stuessy|first4=Tod F|last5=Ricklefs|first5=Robert E|date=2008-10-01|title=Rooting and Dating Maples (Acer) with an Uncorrelated-Rates Molecular Clock: Implications for North American/Asian Disjunctions|journal=Systematic Biology|volume=57|issue=5|pages=795–808|doi=10.1080/10635150802422282|pmid=18853365|issn=1063-5157|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Areces-Berazain|first1=Fabiola|last2=Hinsinger|first2=Damien D.|last3=Strijk|first3=Joeri S.|date=2021-03-01|title=Genome-wide supermatrix analyses of maples (Acer, Sapindaceae) reveal recurring inter-continental migration, mass extinction, and rapid lineage divergence|journal=Genomics|language=en|volume=113|issue=2|pages=681–692|doi=10.1016/j.ygeno.2021.01.014|pmid=33508445|issn=0888-7543|doi-access=free}}</ref> Fifty-four species of maples meet the [[International Union for Conservation of Nature]] criteria for being under threat of extinction in their native habitat.<ref name="Gibbs-2009" />

==Pests and diseases==
[[File:RhytismaAcerinumDetailU.jpg|thumb|''[[Rhytisma acerinum]]'' fungus on ''[[Acer pseudoplatanus]]'' leaf]]
The leaves are used as a food plant for the [[larva]]e of a number of the order [[Lepidoptera]] (see List of Lepidoptera that feed on maples). In high concentrations, caterpillars, like the greenstriped mapleworm (''[[Dryocampa rubicunda]]''), can feed on the leaves so much that they cause temporary defoliation of host maple trees.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://enpp.auburn.edu/outreach/web-publications/greenstriped-mapleworm/|title=Auburn University Entomology and Plant Pathology. Greenstriped Mapleworm|website=Auburn University Entomology and Plant Pathology|language=en|access-date=2017-11-14|archive-date=2017-11-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171103005334/http://enpp.auburn.edu/outreach/web-publications/greenstriped-mapleworm/}}</ref> [[Aphid]]s are also very common sap-feeders on maples, they are a natural part of herbivorous insect communities on maples, though they may become pests when accumulated in large densities.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=McDermot |first1=Covel R. |last2=Minocha |first2=Rakesh |last3=Iii |first3=Vince D'Amico |last4=Long |first4=Stephanie |last5=Trammell |first5=Tara L. E. |date=2020-07-24 |title=Red maple (Acer rubrum L.) trees demonstrate acclimation to urban conditions in deciduous forests embedded in cities |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=15 |issue=7 |article-number=e0236313 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0236313 |doi-access=free |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=7380610 |pmid=32706781 |bibcode=2020PLoSO..1536313M }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Service |date=2015-10-13 |title=Not Found |url=https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/pest-control-tips/aphids.html |access-date=2026-04-07 |website=www.canada.ca}}</ref> In horticultural applications a [[dimethoate]] spray will solve this. 

Aphid abundance has been shown to depend on tree condition and host species.<ref name=":0" />Different maple species support distinct insect communities, one study found that aphid populations were much more abundant on Sycamore maple and lower on Norway maple.<ref name=":0" />Variations in tree health and pest populations are also closely linked as both are influenced by environmental conditions; factors such as urban stress, drought, soil conditions, and pollution can affect tree vitality and alter insect abundance.<ref name=":0" />This relationship is consistent with the plant stress hypothesis which proposes that environmental stress can modify plant defences and, in some cases, increase susceptibility to herbivorous insects.<ref name=":0" />

Infestations of the [[Asian long-horned beetle]] (''Anoplophora glabripennis'') have resulted in the destruction of thousands of maples and other tree species in Illinois, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, and Ohio in the United States and Ontario, Canada.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/259640035|title=Fact Sheets|website=researchgate.net|access-date=19 November 2017}}</ref><ref>[https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/central-park/dailyplant/16597 September 18, 2003 Asian Longhorned Beetle discovered in York Region] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060114221329/http://www.region.york.on.ca/Publications/News/2003/September%2B18%2C%2B2003%2BAsian%2BLonghorned%2BBeetle%2Bdiscovered%2Bin%2BYork%2BRegion.htm |date=January 14, 2006 }}</ref>

Maples are affected by a number of [[fungus|fungal]] diseases. Several are susceptible to Verticillium wilt caused by ''[[Verticillium]]'' species, which can cause significant local mortality. [[Cryptostroma corticale|Sooty bark disease]], caused by ''[[Cryptostroma]]'' species, can kill trees that are under stress due to [[drought]]. Death of maples can rarely be caused by ''[[Phytophthora]]'' [[root rot]] and ''[[Ganoderma]]'' root decay. Maple leaves in late summer and autumn are commonly disfigured by "tar spot" caused by ''[[Rhytisma (fungus)|Rhytisma]]'' species and [[mildew]] caused by ''[[Uncinula]]'' species, though these diseases do not usually have an adverse effect on the trees' long-term health.<ref name="Phillips-1992">Phillips, D. H. & Burdekin, D. A. (1992). ''Diseases of Forest and Ornamental Trees''. Macmillan. {{ISBN|0-333-49493-8}}.</ref>

==Cultural significance==
[[File:Canada flag halifax 9 -04.JPG|thumb|The Canadian flag incorporates a stylized maple leaf]]
[[File:Sammatti.vaakuna.svg|thumb|upright=0.7|The maple leaf and samaras in the coat of arms of [[Sammatti]]]]
A [[maple leaf]] appears on the [[Arms of Canada|coat of arms of Canada]], and is on the [[Canadian flag]]. The maple is a common symbol of strength and endurance and has been chosen as the national tree of Canada. Maple leaves are traditionally an important part of [[Canadian Forces]] military regalia, for example, the military rank insignia for generals use maple leaf symbols. 
There are 10 species naturally growing in the country, with at least one in each province. Although the idea of the tree as a national symbol originally hailed from the province of [[Quebec]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fraser.cc/FlagsCan/Nation/NatSym.html#r10|title=National Symbols|website=The Flag of Canada|date=1998|access-date=19 November 2017|first=Alistair B. |last=Fraser}}</ref> where the [[Acer saccharum|sugar maple]] is significant, today's arboreal emblem of Canada rather refers to a generic maple.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://canada.pch.gc.ca/eng/1444070816842/1444070816844|title=Official symbols of Canada - Canada.ca|first=Canadian|last=Heritage|website=Canada.pch.gc.ca|access-date=19 November 2017}}</ref> The design on the [[Flag of Canada|flag]] is an eleven-point stylization modeled after a sugar maple leaf (which normally bears 23 points).<ref>{{cite book |last1= Sandberg|first1=L. Anders |date= 2014|title=Urban Forests, Trees, and Greenspace: A Political Ecology Perspective|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BRMWBAAAQBAJ&pg=PA182 |publisher=Routledge |isbn= 978-1-134-68763-3}}</ref>

It is also in the name of a Canadian ice hockey team, the [[Toronto Maple Leafs]].

The first attested use of the word was in 1260 as "mapole", and it also appears a century later in [[Geoffrey Chaucer]]'s ''[[Canterbury Tales]]'', spelled as "mapul".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.oed.com/view/Entry/113861|title=maple, n.1|publisher=Oxford University Press|access-date=19 November 2017|via=Oxford English Dictionary}}</ref> The maple is also a symbol of [[Hiroshima]], ubiquitous in the local ''[[meibutsu]]''.

A maple leaf, along with samaras, appears in the coat of arms of [[Sammatti]], a former municipality of [[Uusimaa]], [[Finland]].<ref>{{cite book | title = Suomen kunnallisvaakunat | publisher = Suomen Kunnallisliitto | year = 1982 | page = 161 | isbn = 951-773-085-3 | language = fi}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title = Sisäasiainministeriön vahvistamat kaupunkien, kauppaloiden ja kuntien vaakunat 1949-1995 I:13 Sammatti | url = http://digi.narc.fi/digi/fullpic.ka?kuid=1637005 | publisher = Kansallisarkiston digitaaliarkisto | access-date = September 9, 2021 | language = fi }}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

==Uses==
===Horticulture===
[[File:Maple between pines.jpg|thumb|left|A red maple tree highlighted between [[spruce]] trees]]
[[File:Acer palmatum sango kaku.jpg|thumb|right|''[[Acer palmatum]]'' (Japanese maple) has over 1,000 [[cultivar]]s. This cultivar is ''A. palmatum'' 'Sango kaku', sometimes called "coralbark maple"]]
Some species of maple are extensively planted as [[ornamental tree]]s by homeowners, businesses, and municipalities due to their fall colour, relatively fast growth, ease of transplanting, and lack of hard seeds that would pose a problem for mowing lawns. Particularly popular are [[Norway maple]] (although it is considered invasive in North America), [[silver maple]], [[Japanese maple]], and [[red maple]]. The [[Acer circinatum|vine maple]] is also occasionally used as an ornamental tree. Other maples, especially smaller or more unusual species, are popular as specimen trees.<ref name="van Gelderen-1999"/>

====Cultivars====
Numerous maple [[cultivar]]s that have been selected for particular characteristics can be [[plant propagation|propagated]] only by [[asexual reproduction]] such as cuttings, [[tissue culture]], budding or [[grafting]]. ''[[Acer palmatum]]'' (Japanese maple) alone has over 1,000 cultivars, most selected in Japan, and many of them no longer propagated or not in cultivation in the [[Western world]]. Some delicate cultivars are usually grown in pots and rarely reach heights of more than 50–100&nbsp;cm.
[[File:Japanese Maple 'Kiyohime'.jpg|thumb|Acer palmatum var. 'Kiyohime' as [[bonsai]] during fall [[abscission]]. This dwarf hybrid cultivar is prized for its small leaves and bright red fall colors.]]

====Bonsai====
[[File:Bonsai Federahorn.jpg|thumb|left|"Roter Fächerahorn"]]
Maples are a popular choice for the art of [[bonsai]]. [[Japanese maple]] (''Acer palmatum''), [[trident maple]] (''A. buergerianum''), [[Amur maple]] (''A. ginnala''), [[field maple]] (''A. campestre'') and [[Montpellier maple]] (''A. monspessulanum'') are popular choices and respond well to techniques that encourage leaf reduction and [[ramification (botany)|ramification]], but most species can be used.<ref name="van Gelderen-1999"/><ref name="D'Cruz-2014">{{cite web | first=Mark | last=D'Cruz | title=Ma-Ke Bonsai Care Guide for ''Acer buergerianum'' | publisher=Ma-Ke Bonsai | url=http://makebonsai.com/guide/bonsailink.asp?quicklink=5030&name=Acer_buergerianum | access-date=2011-07-05 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110714022834/http://www.makebonsai.com/guide/bonsailink.asp?quicklink=5030&name=Acer_buergerianum | archive-date=2011-07-14 }}</ref>

====Collections====
[[File:Acer griseum3.jpg|thumb|''[[Acer griseum]]'' is widely grown for its decorative bark]]
Maple collections, sometimes called ''aceretums'', occupy space in many gardens and [[arboretum|arboreta]] around the world including the "five great W's" in [[England]]: [[Wakehurst Place Garden]], [[Westonbirt Arboretum]], [[Windsor Great Park]], [[Winkworth Arboretum]] and [[Wisley Garden]]. In the [[United States]], the aceretum at the [[Harvard University|Harvard]]-owned [[Arnold Arboretum]] in [[Boston, Massachusetts|Boston]] is especially notable. In the number of species and cultivars, the [[Esveld Aceretum]] in [[Boskoop|Boskoop, Netherlands]], is the largest in the world.<ref name="van Gelderen-1999"/>

===Commercial uses===
Maples are important as sources of syrup and wood. Dried wood is often used for the [[Smoking (cooking)|smoking]] of food. Charcoal from maples is an integral part of the [[Lincoln County Process]] used to make [[Tennessee whiskey]].<ref name="Zandona">{{cite web|last=Zandona|first=Eric|title=Tennessee Whiskey Gets a Legal Definition|url=http://www.ezdrinking.com/ezdrinking/2013/9/14/tennessee-whiskey-gets-a-legal-definition|work=EZdrinking|access-date=2014-01-11|archive-date=2014-01-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140107200404/http://www.ezdrinking.com/ezdrinking/2013/9/14/tennessee-whiskey-gets-a-legal-definition}}</ref> They are also cultivated as [[ornamental plant]]s and have benefits for [[tourism]] and [[agriculture]].

====Timber====
[[File:curly maple bench.jpg|thumb|A bench made of highly figured maple wood]]
Some of the larger maple species have valuable [[timber]], particularly Sugar maple in North America and Sycamore maple in Europe. Sugar maple wood—often known as "hard maple"—is the wood of choice for [[bowling]] pins, bowling alley lanes, [[Pool (cue sports)|pool]] and [[snooker]] [[Cue stick|cue shafts]], and [[butcher block|butcher's blocks]]. Maple wood is also used for the manufacture of wooden [[baseball bat]]s, though less often than [[ash (tree)|ash]] or [[hickory]] due to the tendency of maple bats to shatter if they do break. The maple bat was introduced to [[Major League Baseball]] (MLB) in 1998 by [[Sam Bat]] founder Sam Holman. Today it is the standard maple bat most in use by professional baseball.<ref>[http://www.hitrunscore.com/sam-bat-maple-baseball-bat-biography.html Sam Holman Maple Baseball Bats] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100516023403/http://www.hitrunscore.com/sam-bat-maple-baseball-bat-biography.html |date=2010-05-16 }}</ref> Maple is also commonly used in archery as the core material in the limbs of a [[recurve bow]] due to its stiffness and strength.{{citation needed|date = March 2025}}

Maple wood is often graded based on physical and aesthetic characteristics. The most common terminology includes the grading scale from common #2; which is unselected and often used for craft woods; common #1, used for commercial and residential buildings; clear; and select grade, which is sought for fine woodworking.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ahec.org/hardwoods/pdfs/IllustratedGradingGuide.pdf|title=Publications|website=Ahec.org|access-date=19 November 2017|archive-date=24 July 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150724025241/http://ahec.org/hardwoods/pdfs/illustratedgradingguide.pdf}}</ref>

Some maple wood has a highly decorative [[wood grain]], variously known as [[flame maple]], [[quilt maple]], [[birdseye maple]] and [[burl|burl wood]]. This condition occurs randomly in individual trees of several species and often cannot be detected until the wood has been sawn, though it is sometimes visible in the standing tree as a rippled pattern in the bark.{{citation needed|date = March 2025}}

These select decorative wood pieces also have subcategories that further filter the aesthetic looks. Crotch wood, bees wing, cats paw, old growth and mottled are some terms used to describe the look of these decorative woods.<ref>[http://www.hobbithouseinc.com/personal/woodpics/_figure.htm Wood Terms and Examples] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100314144353/http://www.hobbithouseinc.com/personal/woodpics/_figure.htm |date=2010-03-14 }}</ref>

Maples have a long history of use for furniture production in the United States.<ref name="Aronson-1965">{{cite book|author=Joseph Aronson|title=The encyclopedia of furniture|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=j3XWBk-qMV0C&pg=PT300|access-date=8 September 2010|year=1965|publisher=Random House, Inc.|isbn=978-0-517-03735-5|pages=300–}}</ref> The [[Cherokee]] people would produce a purple dye from maple bark, which they used to dye cloth.<ref>{{Citation |contribution=History of the Cherokees, 1830–1846 |title=Chronicles of Oklahoma |last1=Knight |first1=Oliver |publisher=Oklahoma Historical Society|place=Oklahoma City|year=1956–57|page=164|oclc=647927893 |language=en }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author-last=Foreman |author-first=Grant |title=The Five Civilized Tribes |publisher=University of Oklahoma Press |location=Norman |year=1934 |pages=283–284 |language=en |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gGtLnSkqkekC&pg=PA283 |isbn=978-0-8061-0923-7 }}</ref>

====Tonewood====
Maple is considered a [[tonewood]], or a wood that carries sound waves well, and is used in numerous [[musical instrument]]s. Maple is harder and has a brighter sound than [[mahogany]], which is another major tonewood used in instrument manufacturing.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.fender.com/en-GB/news/index.php/?display_article=395 |title=Archived copy |access-date=2012-11-14 |archive-date=2021-03-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210302174809/https://www.fender.com/en-GB/news/index.php/?display_article=395 }}</ref>

The back, sides, and neck of most [[violin]]s, [[viola]]s, [[cello]]s, and [[double bass]]es are made from maple.<ref>{{cite book |last=Bucur |first=Voichita |title=Handbook of Materials for String Musical Instruments |chapter=Description of String Instruments for Classical Music |publisher=Springer |location=Cham |year=2016 |pages=43–45 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-32080-9_2 |isbn=978-3-319-32080-9 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-32080-9_2}}</ref>

[[Electric guitar]] necks are commonly made from maple, having good dimensional stability. The necks of the Fender [[Stratocaster]] and [[Telecaster]] were originally an entirely maple one piece neck, but later were also available with [[rosewood]] fingerboards. [[Les Paul]] desired an all maple guitar, but due to the weight of maple, only the tops of [[Gibson Guitar Corporation|Gibson]]'s Les Paul guitars are made from carved maple, often using quilted or flamed maple tops. Due to its weight, very few [[solid body]] guitars are made entirely from maple, but many guitars have maple necks, tops or veneers.{{citation needed|date = March 2025}}

Maple is also often used to make [[bassoon]]s and sometimes other [[woodwind instrument]]s such as [[recorder (musical_instrument)|recorder]]s.<ref>{{cite book |last=Bucur |first=Voichita |title=Handbook of Materials for Wind Musical Instruments |chapter=Wood Species for Reed-Driven Instruments—Clarinet, Oboe, Bassoon and for Baroque Flute |publisher=Springer |location=Cham |year=2019 |pages=127–166 |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-19175-7_3 |isbn=978-3-030-19175-7 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-19175-7_3}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Types of Wood for Recorders |url=https://www.vonhuene.com/t-recorderwood.aspx |website=The Von Huene Workshop |access-date=2026-04-18}}</ref>

Many [[drum]]s are made from maple. From the 1970s to the 1990s, maple drum kits were a vast majority of all drum kits made, but in recent years, [[birch]] has become popular for drums once again. Some of the best drum-building companies use maple extensively throughout their mid-pro range.<ref name="van Gelderen-1999"/> Maple drums are favored for their bright resonant sound.<ref name="Nicholls-1997">{{cite book|author1=Geoff Nicholls|author2=Tony Bacon|title=The drum book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rWq1_qnZ0mAC&pg=PT54|access-date=19 October 2010|date=1 June 1997|publisher=Hal Leonard Corporation|isbn=978-0-87930-476-8|pages=54–}}</ref> Certain drum sticks are also made from maple.<ref>{{cite web |last=Wengert |first=Gene |title=Tips for young drummers about wooden drumsticks |website=Woodworking Network |date=2012-11-14 |url=https://www.woodworkingnetwork.com/magazine/fdmc-magazine/tips-young-drummers-about-wooden-drumsticks}}</ref>

====Agriculture====
During late winter to early spring in northeastern [[North America]], when the night-to-day temperatures change from freezing to thawing, maple trees may be tapped for [[sap]] to manufacture [[maple syrup]].<ref name="QMSP-2021">{{cite web|url=https://ppaq.ca/en/maple-production/step-by-step-production-maple-syrup/ |title=Step-by-Step in the Production of Maple Syrup |publisher=Québec Maple Syrup Producers |date=2021|access-date=4 October 2021}}</ref> The sap is sent via tubing to a [[sugar house]] where it is boiled to produce syrup or made into [[maple sugar]] or [[maple taffy]]. It takes about {{convert|40|L|USqt}} of sugar maple sap to make {{convert|1|L|USqt}} of syrup.<ref name="QMSP-2021"/> While any ''Acer'' species may be tapped for syrup, many do not have sufficient quantities of sugar to be commercially useful, whereas [[sugar maple]]s (''A. saccharum'') are most commonly used to produce maple syrup.<ref name="QMSP-2021"/> [[Quebec]] is a major producer of maple syrup, an industry worth about 500 million [[Canadian dollars]] annually.<ref name="QMSP-2021"/><ref name="Marowits-2017">{{cite web|url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/quebec-maple-syrup-production-increase-1.3990828|title=Quebec increases maple syrup production amid internal revolt, foreign competition|author=Marowits, Ross|publisher=CBC|date=20 February 2017|access-date=21 May 2017|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170518192634/http://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/quebec-maple-syrup-production-increase-1.3990828|archive-date=18 May 2017|df=dmy-all}}</ref>

Also, as these trees are a major source of [[pollen]] in early spring before many other plants have flowered, maple flowers are a source of foraging for [[honeybee]]s that play a commercially important role in general agriculture and in natural habitats.<ref name="ArborDay-2021">{{cite web |title=Trees for bees and other pollinators |url=https://www.arborday.org/trees/health/pests/article-trees-for-bees.cfm |publisher=Arbor Day Foundation |access-date=5 October 2021 |date=2021}}</ref>

====Pulpwood====
Maple is used as [[pulpwood]]. The fibers have relatively thick walls that prevent collapsing upon drying. This gives good bulk and [[opacity]] in [[paper]]. With a lignin content of approximately 21%, maple is often processed into high yield pulp to enhance printing properties.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=He Shi |last2=Hongbin Liu |last3=Yonghao Ni |last4=Zhirun Yuan |last5=Xuejun Zou |last6=Zhou |first6=Yajun |date=2012-05-01 |title=REVIEW: USE OF OPTICAL BRIGHTENING AGENTS (OBAs) IN THE PRODUCTION OF PAPER CONTAINING HIGH-YIELD PULPS |url=http://ojs.cnr.ncsu.edu/index.php/BioRes/article/view/BioRes_07_2_2582_Shi_LNYZZ_Review_OBAs_High_Yield_Pulp/1529 |journal=BioResources |language=en |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=2582–2591 |issn=1930-2126}}</ref>

===Tourism===
Many maples have bright [[autumn foliage]], and many countries have leaf-watching traditions. The sugar maple (''[[Acer saccharum]]''), whose leaves turn brilliant orange, is the primary contributor to fall "[[leaf peeping|foliage season]]" in north-eastern [[North America]]. In [[Japan]], the custom of viewing the changing colour of maples in the autumn is called [[Leaf peeping|''momijigari'']]. [[Nikkō]] and [[Kyoto]] are particularly favoured destinations for this activity. In Korea, the same viewing activity is called ''danpung-nori'' and the [[Seoraksan]] and [[Naejang-san]] mountains are among the best-known destinations. These are examples of [[Ecosystem service|ecosystem services]] are examples of cultural [[Ecosystem service|ecosystem services]] that hold relational value.<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://zenodo.org/record/6522392 |title=Summary for policymakers of the methodological assessment of the diverse values and valuation of nature of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) |last=Unai |first=Pascual |date=2022-07-09 |publisher=Zenodo |doi=10.5281/zenodo.6522392 |language=en}}</ref>

======================================================================
ARTICLE: Medicinal plants
WIKIPEDIA REVISION TEXT
======================================================================

{{short description|Plants used to treat medical conditions}}
{{good article}}
{{Use British English|date=September 2021}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2025}}
[[File:Salix alba 004.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|The bark of [[willow]] trees contains [[salicylic acid]], the [[active metabolite]] of [[aspirin]], and has been used for millennia to [[pain reliever|relieve pain]] and reduce [[fever]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Lichterman |first=B. L. |title=Aspirin: The Story of a Wonder Drug |journal=[[British Medical Journal]] |year=2004 |volume=329 |issue=7479 |page=1408 |doi=10.1136/bmj.329.7479.1408 |pmc=535471}}</ref>]]

'''Medicinal plants''', also called '''medicinal herbs''', have been discovered and used in [[traditional medicine]] practices since prehistoric times. [[Plants]] synthesize hundreds of chemical compounds for various functions, including [[Plant defense against herbivory|defense]] and protection against [[insect]]s, [[fungi]], [[Plant disease resistance|diseases]], against [[parasite]]s<ref>{{cite journal |last1=François |first1=G. |last2=Steenackers |first2=T. |last3=Assi |first3=L. A. |display-authors=etal |date=1999 |issue=7 |pages=582–588 https://doi.org/10.1007/s004360050598 |journal=Parasitology Research |title=Vismione H and structurally related anthranoid compounds of natural and synthetic origin as promising drugs against the human malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum: structure-activity relationships |volume=85|doi=10.1007/s004360050598 |pmid=10382608 }}<!-- auto-translated from German by Module:CS1 translator --></ref> and [[herbivorous]] [[mammal]]s.<ref name="gers">{{cite journal |last1=Gershenzon |first1=J. |last2=Ullah |first2=C. |title=Plants protect themselves from herbivores by optimizing the distribution of chemical defenses |journal=PNAS |volume=119 |issue=4 |date=January 2022 |article-number=e2120277119 |pmid=35084361 |pmc=8794845 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2120277119|doi-access=free |bibcode=2022PNAS..11920277G }}</ref>

The earliest historical records of herbs are found from the [[Sumer]]ian civilization, where hundreds of medicinal plants including [[opium]] are listed on clay tablets, {{circa|3000 BC}}. The [[Ebers Papyrus]] from [[ancient Egypt]], {{circa|1550 BC}}, describes over 850 plant medicines. The Greek physician [[Pedanius Dioscorides|Dioscorides]], who worked in the Roman army, documented over 1000 recipes for medicines using over 600 medicinal plants in {{lang|la|[[De materia medica]]}}, {{circa|60 AD}}; this formed the basis of [[pharmacopoeia]]s for some 1500 years. Drug research sometimes makes use of [[ethnobotany]] to search for pharmacologically active substances, and this approach has yielded hundreds of useful compounds. These include the common drugs [[aspirin]], [[digoxin]], [[quinine]], and opium. The compounds found in plants are diverse, with most in four biochemical classes: [[alkaloid]]s, [[glycoside]]s, [[polyphenol]]s, and [[terpene]]s. Few of these are [[evidence-based medicine|scientifically confirmed as medicines]] or used in conventional medicine.

Medicinal plants are widely used as folk medicine in non-industrialized societies, mainly because they are readily available and cheaper than modern medicines. In many countries, there is little regulation of traditional medicine, but the [[World Health Organization]] coordinates a network to encourage safe and rational use. The botanical herbal market has been criticized for being poorly regulated and containing [[placebo]] and [[pseudoscience]] products with no scientific research to support their medical claims.<ref name="ahn">{{cite journal |last=Ahn |first=K. |title=The worldwide trend of using botanical drugs and strategies for developing global drugs |journal=BMB Reports |year=2017 |volume=50 |issue=3 |pages=111–116 |doi=10.5483/BMBRep.2017.50.3.221 |pmid=27998396 |pmc=5422022 }}</ref> Medicinal plants face both general threats, such as [[climate change]] and [[habitat destruction]], and the specific threat of over-collection to meet market demand.<ref name=ahn/>
<!--

-->

==History==

[[File:PEbers c41-bc.jpg|thumb|upright|The [[Ebers Papyrus]] ({{circa|1550 BC}}) from [[Ancient Egypt]] describes the use of hundreds of plant medicines.<ref name="Sumner-2000-p17"/>]]

[[File:Arabic herbal medicine guidebook.jpeg|thumb|[[Dioscorides]]'s 1st century {{lang|la|[[De materia medica]]}}, seen here in a {{circa|1334}} copy in Arabic, describes some 1000 drug recipes based on over 600 plants.<ref name=Collins2000/>]]

{{further|History of herbalism|History of pharmacy}}

===Prehistoric times===

Plants, including many now used as [[culinary herb]]s and [[spice]]s, have been used as medicines, not necessarily effectively, from prehistoric times. Spices have been used partly to counter [[food spoilage]] bacteria, especially in hot climates,<ref name="tapsell" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Billing |first1=Jennifer |last2=Sherman |first2=P. W. |title=Antimicrobial functions of spices: why some like it hot |journal=[[Quarterly Review of Biology]] |volume=73 |issue=1 |pages=3–49 |date=March 1998 |doi=10.1086/420058 |pmid=9586227 |s2cid=22420170 }}</ref> and especially in meat dishes that spoil more readily.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sherman |first1=P. W. |last2=Hash |first2=G. A. |title=Why vegetable recipes are not very spicy |journal=Evolution and Human Behavior |volume=22 |issue=3 |pages=147–163 |date=May 2001 |doi=10.1016/S1090-5138(00)00068-4 |pmid=11384883 |bibcode=2001EHumB..22..147S }}</ref> Angiosperms ([[flowering plant]]s) were the original source of most plant medicines.<ref name="Angio">{{cite encyclopedia |title=Angiosperms: Division Magnoliophyta: General Features |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopædia Britannica]] (volume 13, 15th edition) |year=1993 |page=609 }}</ref> Human settlements are often surrounded by weeds used as [[herbal medicine]]s, such as [[Urtica dioica|nettle]], [[dandelion]] and [[chickweed]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Stepp |first=John R. |title=The role of weeds as sources of pharmaceuticals |journal=[[Journal of Ethnopharmacology]] |volume=92 |issue=2–3 |pages=163–166 |date=June 2004 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2004.03.002 |pmid=15137997}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Stepp |first1=John R. |last2=Moerman |first2=Daniel E. |title=The importance of weeds in ethnopharmacology |journal=[[Journal of Ethnopharmacology]] |volume=75 |issue=1 |pages=19–23 |date=April 2001 |doi=10.1016/S0378-8741(00)00385-8 |pmid=11282438}}</ref> Humans were not alone in using herbs: some animals, such as non-human [[primate]]s, [[Monarch butterfly|monarch butterflies]] and [[sheep]] ingest plants when they are ill.<ref>{{cite book |author=Sumner, Judith |title=The Natural History of Medicinal Plants |publisher=[[Timber Press]] |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-88192-483-1 |page=16}}</ref>

Samples from prehistoric burial sites indicate that Paleolithic peoples consumed plants. For instance, a 60,000-year-old Neanderthal burial site, "[[Shanidar Cave#Shanidar 4.2C the .22flower burial.22|Shanidar IV]]", in northern Iraq yielded pollen from eight plant species.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Solecki |first=Ralph S. |title=Shanidar IV, a Neanderthal Flower Burial in Northern Iraq |journal=Science |volume=190 |issue=4217 |date=November 1975 |pages=880–881 |doi=10.1126/science.190.4217.880 |bibcode=1975Sci...190..880S |s2cid=71625677 }}</ref> At [[Taforalt]] cave, Morocco, 15,000-year-old remains of [[Ephedra (plant)|ephedra]] were found inside a tomb, indicating its possible role in funeral rites.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Morales |first1=Jacob |last2=Carrión Marco |first2=Yolanda |last3=Cooper |first3=Joanne H. |last4=Turner |first4=Elaine |last5=Freyne |first5=Alison |last6=Hogue |first6=Joshua |last7=Ziani |first7=Ismail |last8=Barton |first8=R. Nicholas E. |last9=Bouzouggar |first9=Abdeljalil |last10=Humphrey |first10=Louise T. |display-authors=3|date=2024-11-02 |title=Late pleistocene exploitation of Ephedra in a funerary context in Morocco |journal=Scientific Reports |language=en |volume=14 |issue=1 |page=26443 |doi=10.1038/s41598-024-77785-w  |doi-access=free|issn=2045-2322 |pmc=11531600 |pmid=39488593 |bibcode=2024NatSR..1426443M }}</ref> A mushroom found in the personal effects of ''[[Ötzi the Iceman]]'', whose body was frozen in the [[Ötztal Alps]] for more than 5,000 years, may have been used against [[whipworm]].<ref name="pmid9851424">{{cite journal |author=Capasso, L. |title=5300 years ago, the Ice Man used natural laxatives and antibiotics |journal=Lancet |volume=352 |issue=9143 |page=1864 |date=December 1998 |pmid=9851424 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(05)79939-6 |s2cid=40027370 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

===Ancient times===

In ancient [[Sumer]]ia, hundreds of medicinal plants including [[myrrh]] and opium are listed on clay tablets from around 3000 BC. The [[Ancient Egyptian medicine|ancient Egyptian]] [[Ebers Papyrus]] lists over 800 plant medicines such as [[aloe]], [[cannabis]], [[castor bean]], [[garlic]], [[juniper]], and [[Mandragora (genus)|mandrake]].<ref name="Sumner-2000-p17">{{cite book |last=Sumner |first=Judith |title=The Natural History of Medicinal Plants |publisher=[[Timber Press]] |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-88192-483-1|page=17}}</ref>{{sfn|Petrovska|2012|pp=1–5}}

From ancient times to the present, [[Ayurveda|Ayurvedic medicine]] as documented in the [[Atharva Veda]], the [[Rig Veda]] and the [[Sushruta Samhita]] has used hundreds of herbs and spices, such as [[turmeric]], which contains [[curcumin]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Dwivedi |first1=Girish |last2=Dwivedi |first2=Shridhar |year=2007 |title=History of Medicine: Sushruta – the Clinician – Teacher par Excellence |publisher=[[National Informatics Centre]] |url=http://medind.nic.in/iae/t07/i4/iaet07i4p243.pdf |access-date=8 October 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081010045900/http://medind.nic.in/iae/t07/i4/iaet07i4p243.pdf |archive-date=10 October 2008 }}</ref> The [[Chinese herbology|Chinese pharmacopoeia]], the ''[[Shennong Ben Cao Jing]]'' records plant medicines such as [[chaulmoogra]] for leprosy, [[Ephedra (medicine)|ephedra]], and [[hemp]].<ref name="Sumner-2000-p18">{{cite book |last=Sumner |first=Judith |title=The Natural History of Medicinal Plants |publisher=[[Timber Press]] |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-88192-483-1 |page=18}}</ref> This was expanded in the [[Tang dynasty]] ''[[Yaoxing Lun]]''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Wu |first=Jing-Nuan |title=An Illustrated Chinese Materia Medica |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |year=2005 |isbn=978-0-19-514017-0 |page=6 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=H9Q8agQrJR0C&pg=PA6}}</ref> In the fourth century BC, [[Aristotle]]'s pupil [[Theophrastus]] wrote the first systematic botany text, ''[[Historia Plantarum (Theophrastus)|Historia plantarum]]''.<ref name="philobio11">{{cite book |last=Grene |first=Marjorie |title=The philosophy of biology: an episodic history |year=2004 |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |isbn=978-0-521-64380-1 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TJSGJjh8Jo8C&pg=PA11 |page=11}}</ref>

In around 60 AD, the Greek physician [[Dioscorides]], working for the Roman army, documented over 1000 recipes for medicines using over 600 medicinal plants in {{lang|la|[[De materia medica]]}}. The book remained the authoritative reference on herbalism for over 1500 years, into the seventeenth century.<ref name=Collins2000>{{cite book |last=Collins |first=Minta |title=Medieval Herbals: The Illustrative Traditions |publisher=[[University of Toronto Press]] |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-8020-8313-5 |page=32 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=s7c2EaxDYjUC&pg=PA32}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Osbaldeston |first=Tess Anne |title=De materia medica - Pedanius Dioscorides - |url=http://www.cancerlynx.com/dioscorides.html |access-date=11 November 2022 |date=2008}}</ref>

===Middle Ages===

[[File:Physician talking to a female patient in a garden Wellcome L0073711.jpg|thumb|upright|Illustration of a 1632 copy of [[Avicenna]]'s 1025 ''[[The Canon of Medicine]]'', showing a physician talking to a female patient in a garden, while servants prepare medicines.]]<!--image for 'Middle Ages'-->

In the [[Early Middle Ages]], [[Benedictine monasteries]] preserved medical knowledge in [[Europe]], translating and copying classical texts and maintaining [[herb garden]]s.<ref>{{cite book |last=Arsdall |first=Anne V. |title=Medieval Herbal Remedies: The Old English Herbarium and Anglo-Saxon Medicine |publisher=Psychology Press |year=2002 |isbn=978-0-415-93849-5 |pages=70–71 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ITxsaqEmVHAC&pg=PA70}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Mills |first=Frank A. |chapter=Botany |editor=Johnston, William M. |title=Encyclopedia of Monasticism: M-Z |publisher=[[Taylor & Francis]] |year=2000 |isbn=978-1-57958-090-2 |page=179 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GfC0TDkJJNgC&pg=PA179}}</ref> [[Hildegard of Bingen]] wrote ''Causae et Curae'' ("Causes and Cures") on medicine.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Ramos-e-Silva Marcia |year=1999 |title=Saint Hildegard Von Bingen (1098–1179) "The Light Of Her People And Of Her Time" |journal=International Journal of Dermatology |volume=38 |issue=4 |pages=315–320 |doi=10.1046/j.1365-4362.1999.00617.x |pmid=10321953 |s2cid=13404562 }}</ref>

In the [[Islamic Golden Age]], scholars translated many classical Greek texts including Dioscorides into [[Arabic]], adding their own commentaries.<ref>{{cite book |title=The New Healing Herbs |last=Castleman |first=Michael |publisher=Rodale |year=2001 |page=[https://archive.org/details/newhealingherbs00mich/page/15 15] |isbn=978-1-57954-304-4 |url=https://archive.org/details/newhealingherbs00mich/page/15 }}; {{cite book |last=Collins |first=Minta |title=Medieval Herbals: The Illustrative Traditions |publisher=[[University of Toronto Press]] |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-8020-8313-5 |page=115 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=s7c2EaxDYjUC&pg=PA115 }}; {{cite web |url=https://www.nlm.nih.gov/exhibition/islamic_medical/islamic_11.html |title=Pharmaceutics and Alchemy |publisher=US National Library of Medicine |access-date=26 January 2017 |archive-date=5 January 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170105140717/https://www.nlm.nih.gov/exhibition/islamic_medical/islamic_11.html |url-status=live }}; {{cite book |last=Fahd |first=Toufic |title=Botany and agriculture |page=815}}, in {{cite book |last1=Rashed |first1=Roshdi |last2=Morelon |first2=Régis |title=Encyclopedia of the History of Arabic Science: Astronomy-Theoretical and applied, v.2 Mathematics and the physical sciences; v.3 Technology, alchemy and life sciences |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Fx7GtwAACAAJ |year=1996 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-02063-3 }}</ref>
Herbalism flourished in the Islamic world, particularly in [[Baghdad]] and in [[Al-Andalus]]. Among many works on medicinal plants, [[Abulcasis]] (936–1013) of [[Córdoba, Spain|Cordoba]] wrote ''The Book of Simples'', and Ibn al-Baitar (1197–1248) recorded hundreds of medicinal herbs such as ''Aconitum'', [[nux vomica (herbalism)|nux vomica]], and [[tamarind]] in his ''Corpus of Simples''.<ref name=Castlemanp15>{{cite book |title=The New Healing Herbs |last=Castleman |first=Michael |publisher=Rodale |year=2001 |page=[https://archive.org/details/newhealingherbs00mich/page/15 15] |isbn=978-1-57954-304-4 |url=https://archive.org/details/newhealingherbs00mich/page/15 }}</ref> [[Avicenna]] included many plants in his 1025 ''[[The Canon of Medicine]]''.<ref name=Jacquart>{{cite journal |last=Jacquart |first=Danielle |journal=European Review |volume=16 |issue=2 |pages=219–227 [223] |year=2008 |title=Islamic Pharmacology in the Middle Ages: Theories and Substances |doi=10.1017/S1062798708000215 }}</ref> [[Abu-Rayhan Biruni]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kujundzić |first1=E. |author2=Masić, I. |title=[Al-Biruni--a universal scientist] |journal=Medical Archives |date=1999 |volume=53 |issue=2 |pages=117–120 |language=hr |pmid=10386051}}</ref> [[Ibn Zuhr]],<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1086/372742 |last1=Krek |first1=M. |year=1979 |title=The Enigma of the First Arabic Book Printed from Movable Type |journal=Journal of Near Eastern Studies |volume=38 |issue=3|pages=203–212 |s2cid=162374182 }}</ref> [[Peter of Spain (author)|Peter of Spain]], and [[John of St Amand]] wrote further [[pharmacopoeia]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1067/mcp.2000.106465 |last1=Brater |first1=D. Craig |author2=Daly, Walter J. |year=2000 |title=Clinical pharmacology in the Middle Ages: Principles that presage the 21st century | journal=Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics |volume=67 |issue=5|pages=447–450 [448–449] |pmid=10824622|s2cid=45980791 }}</ref>

===Early Modern===

[[File:The Grete Herball, Title Page, 1526.jpg|thumb|upright|An early illustrated book of medicinal plants,<ref name=Singer/> ''[[The Grete Herball]]'', 1526]]

The [[Early Modern]] period saw the flourishing of illustrated [[herbal]]s across Europe, starting with the 1526 ''[[Grete Herball]]''. [[John Gerard]] wrote his famous ''The Herball or General History of Plants'' in 1597, based on [[Rembert Dodoens]], and [[Nicholas Culpeper]] published his ''The English Physician Enlarged''.<ref name=Singer>{{cite journal |author-link=Charles Singer |last=Singer |first=Charles |date=1923 |title=Herbals |journal=[[The Edinburgh Review]] |volume=237 |pages=95–112}}</ref> 
Many new plant medicines arrived in Europe as products of [[Age of Exploration|Early Modern exploration]] and the resulting [[Columbian Exchange]], in which livestock, crops and technologies were transferred between the Old World and the Americas in the 15th and 16th centuries. Medicinal herbs arriving in the Americas included garlic, ginger, and turmeric; coffee, tobacco and coca travelled in the other direction.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nunn |first1=Nathan |last2=Qian |first2=Nancy |year= 2010 |title=The Columbian Exchange: A History of Disease, Food, and Ideas |journal=[[Journal of Economic Perspectives]] |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=163–188 |jstor=25703506 |doi=10.1257/jep.24.2.163  |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Heywood |first1=Vernon H. |title=The role of New World biodiversity in the transformation of Mediterranean landscapes and culture |url=http://147.163.105.223/bocconea/24-069.pdf |journal=Bocconea |volume=24 |pages=69–93 |date=2012 |access-date=2017-02-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170227062205/http://147.163.105.223/bocconea/24-069.pdf |archive-date=2017-02-27 }}</ref>
In Mexico, the sixteenth century ''Badianus Manuscript'' described medicinal plants available in Central America.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Gimmel Millie |year=2008 |title=Reading Medicine In The Codex De La Cruz Badiano |journal=Journal of the History of Ideas |volume=69 |issue=2|pages=169–192 |doi=10.1353/jhi.2008.0017|pmid=19127831 |s2cid=46457797 }}</ref><!--<ref>{{cite book |author=Kremers, Edward |title=Kremers and Urdang's History of Pharmacy |publisher=Amer. Inst. History of Pharmacy |year=1986 |isbn=978-0-931292-17-0 |page=40 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=r__FmMNS7qIC&pg=PA40 |display-authors=etal}}</ref>-->

===19th and 20th centuries===

{{further|Pharmacognosy}}

The place of plants in medicine was radically altered in the 19th century by the application of [[chemistry|chemical analysis]]. [[Alkaloid]]s were isolated from a succession of medicinal plants, starting with [[morphine]] from the [[poppy]] in 1806, and soon followed by [[Cephaelis ipecacuanha|ipecacuanha]] and [[strychnos]] in 1817, [[quinine]] from the [[cinchona]] tree, and then many others. As chemistry progressed, additional classes of potentially active substances were discovered in plants. Commercial extraction of purified alkaloids including morphine began at [[Merck Group|Merck]] in 1826. [[Organic synthesis|Synthesis]] of a substance first discovered in a medicinal plant began with salicylic acid in 1853. Around the end of the 19th century, the mood of pharmacy turned against medicinal plants, as [[enzyme]]s often modified the active ingredients when whole plants were dried, and alkaloids and glycosides purified from plant material started to be preferred. Drug discovery from plants continued to be important through the 20th century and into the 21st, with important anti-cancer drugs from [[yew]] and [[Madagascar periwinkle]].<ref name=Atanasov2015/><ref name="Petrovska 2012">{{cite journal |last=Petrovska |first=Biljana Bauer |title=Historical review of medicinal plants' usage |journal=Pharmacognosy Reviews |date=2012 |volume=6 |issue=11 |pages=1–5 |doi=10.4103/0973-7847.95849 |pmid=22654398 |pmc=3358962 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=APS>{{Citation |last1=Price |first1=J. R. |author2=Lamberton, J. A. |author3=Culvenor, C.C.J. |title=The Australian Phytochemical Survey: historical aspects of the CSIRO search for new drugs in Australian plants. Historical Records of Australian Science, 9(4), 335–356 |journal=Historical Records of Australian Science |year=1992 |volume=9 |issue=4 |publication-date=1992 |publisher=Australian Academy of Science |url=https://www.publish.csiro.au/HR/HR9930940335 |pages=335–356 |doi=10.1071/hr9930940335 |access-date=2022-04-02 |archive-date=2022-01-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220121231103/https://www.publish.csiro.au/hr/HR9930940335 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Context==

Medicinal plants are used with the intention of maintaining health, to be administered for a specific condition, or both, whether in [[medicine|modern medicine]] or in traditional medicine.<ref name=ahn/><ref name=Smith-Hall2012>{{cite journal |last1=Smith-Hall |first1=C. |author2=Larsen, H.O. |author3=Pouliot, M. |title=People, plants and health: a conceptual framework for assessing changes in medicinal plant consumption |journal=J Ethnobiol Ethnomed |volume=8 |article-number=43 |year=2012 |pmid=23148504 |pmc=3549945 |doi=10.1186/1746-4269-8-43 |doi-access=free }}</ref> The [[Food and Agriculture Organization]] estimated in 2002 that over 50,000 medicinal plants are used across the world.<ref name="FAO">{{cite web |last1=Schippmann |first1=Uwe |last2=Leaman |first2=Danna J. |last3=Cunningham |first3=A. B. |title=Impact of Cultivation and Gathering of Medicinal Plants on Biodiversity: Global Trends and Issues 2. Some Figures to start with ... |work=Biodiversity and the Ecosystem Approach in Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries. Satellite event on the occasion of the Ninth Regular Session of the Commission on Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture. Rome, 12–13 October 2002. Inter-Departmental Working Group on Biological Diversity for Food and Agriculture. Rome |url=http://www.fao.org/docrep/005/AA010E/AA010e02.htm |publisher=Food and Agriculture Organization |access-date=25 September 2017 |date=12 October 2002 |archive-date=24 July 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170724135111/http://www.fao.org/docrep/005/AA010E/AA010e02.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> The [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] more conservatively estimated in 2016 that 17,810 plant species have a medicinal use, out of some 30,000 plants for which a use of any kind is documented.<ref name="Kew2016">{{cite web|title=State of the World's Plants Report - 2016|url=https://stateoftheworldsplants.com/2016/report/sotwp_2016.pdf|publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|access-date=25 September 2017|date=2016|archive-date=19 September 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170919052314/https://stateoftheworldsplants.com/2016/report/sotwp_2016.pdf}}</ref>

In modern medicine, around a quarter{{efn|Farnsworth states that this figure was based on prescriptions from American community pharmacies between 1959 and 1980.<ref name=Farnsworth1985/>}} of the drugs prescribed to patients are derived from medicinal plants, and they are rigorously tested.<ref name=Smith-Hall2012/><ref name=Farnsworth1985/> In other systems of medicine, medicinal plants may constitute the majority of what are often informal attempted treatments, not tested scientifically.<ref name="Tilburt 2008">{{cite journal |last1=Tilburt |first1=Jon C. |last2=Kaptchuk |first2=Ted J. |title=Herbal medicine research and global health: an ethical analysis |journal=Bulletin of the World Health Organization |date=August 2008 |volume=86 |issue=8 |pages=577–656 |doi=10.2471/BLT.07.042820 |pmid=18797616 |pmc=2649468 |url=https://www.who.int/bulletin/volumes/86/8/07-042820/en/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100124091134/http://www.who.int/bulletin/volumes/86/8/07-042820/en/ |archive-date=January 24, 2010 |access-date=22 September 2017 }}</ref> The [[World Health Organization]] estimates, without reliable data, that some 80 percent of the world's population depends mainly on traditional medicine (including but not limited to plants); perhaps some two billion people are largely reliant on medicinal plants.<ref name=Smith-Hall2012/><ref name=Farnsworth1985>{{cite journal |last1=Farnsworth |first1=Norman R. |last2=Akerele |first2=Olayiwola |last3=Bingel |first3=Audrey S. |last4=Soejarto |first4=Djada D. |last5=Guo |first5=Zhengang |title=Medicinal plants in therapy |journal=Bulletin of the World Health Organization |date=1985 |volume=63 |issue=6|pages=965–981|pmid=3879679 |pmc=2536466 }}</ref> The use of plant-based materials including herbal or natural health products with supposed health benefits, is increasing in developed countries.<ref name=Ekor2013>{{cite journal |last1=Ekor |first1=Martins |title=The growing use of herbal medicines: issues relating to adverse reactions and challenges in monitoring safety |journal=Frontiers in Pharmacology |date=2013 |volume=4 |issue=3 |pages=202–4|doi=10.3389/fphar.2013.00177 |pmid=24454289 |pmc=3887317|doi-access=free }}</ref> This brings attendant risks of toxicity and other effects on human health, despite the safe image of herbal remedies.<ref name=Ekor2013/> Herbal medicines have been in use since long before modern medicine existed; there was and often still is little or no knowledge of the pharmacological basis of their actions, if any, or of their safety. The World Health Organization formulated a policy on traditional medicine in 1991, and since then has published guidelines for them, with a series of monographs on widely used herbal medicines.<ref>{{cite book |last=Singh |first=Amritpal |title=Regulatory and Pharmacological Basis of Ayurvedic Formulations |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zgBPDAAAQBAJ&pg=PA4 |date=2016 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-1-4987-5096-7 |pages=4–5}}</ref><ref name=Cravotto/>
[[File:Drying herbs - Lamium purpureum.jpg|thumb|Drying a common [[weed]], [[Lamium purpureum|red dead-nettle]], as a [[medicinal plant]] in a [[wicker]] basket, [[Poland]]]]
Medicinal plants may provide three main kinds of benefit: health benefits to the people who consume them as medicines; financial benefits to people who harvest, process, and distribute them for sale; and society-wide benefits, such as job opportunities, taxation income, and a healthier labour force.<ref name=Smith-Hall2012/> However, development of plants or extracts having potential medicinal uses is blunted by weak scientific evidence, poor practices in the process of [[drug development]], and insufficient financing.<ref name=ahn/><ref name=Berida_2024>{{cite journal | vauthors=Berida T, Adekunle Y, Dada-Adegbola H, Kdimy A, Roy S, Sarker S | title=Plant antibacterials: The challenges and opportunities | journal=Heliyon | volume=10 | issue=10 | article-number=e31145 | date=May 2024 | pmid=38803958 | pmc=11128932 | doi=10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e31145 | bibcode=2024Heliy..1031145B | doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Trade==

The markets for medicinal and [[odor|aromatic]] plants are grouped in manufacturing categories of pharmaceuticals and dietary supplements, food and beverages, personal care products and cosmetics, with the pharmaceutical and supplement category accounting for about 60% of the total.<ref name="zamani">{{cite journal |vauthors=Zamani S, Fathi M, Ebadi M, Máthé A |title=Global trade of medicinal and aromatic plants. A review |journal=Journal of Agriculture and Food Research |date=2025 |volume=21 |article-number=101910 |doi=10.1016/j.jafr.2025.101910 |doi-access=free }}</ref> As of 2023 by one estimate, the global market was US$68 billion per year, growing by 10-20% annually.<ref name=zamani/>

China and India are the leading producers of natural products, and are also the leading exporters and domestic consumers.<ref name=zamani/> Major importers include the United States, the European Union, and Japan.<ref name=zamani/>

==Phytochemical basis==

{{further|Phytochemistry}}

All plants produce chemical compounds which give them an [[evolution]]ary advantage, such as [[Plant defense against herbivory|defending against herbivores]] or, in the example of salicylic acid, as a [[plant hormone|hormone]] in plant defenses.<ref name=USDAingredients/><ref>{{cite book |title=Salicylic Acid – A Plant Hormone |last1=Hayat |first1=S. |author2=Ahmad, A. |isbn=978-1-4020-5183-8 |year=2007 |publisher=Springer Science and Business Media |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/salicylicacidpla0000unse }}</ref> These phytochemicals have potential for use as drugs,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lamottke |first1=Kai |last2=Ripoll |first2=Christophe |last3=Walczak |first3=Robert |date=2011 |pages=52–56 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/260943788 |journal=European Biopharmaceutical Review |title=The roots of innovation |volume=15}}<!-- auto-translated from German by Module:CS1 translator --></ref> and the content and known pharmacological activity of these substances in medicinal plants is the scientific basis for their use in modern medicine, if scientifically confirmed.<ref name=ahn/> For instance, daffodils (''[[Narcissus (plant)|Narcissus]]'') contain nine groups of alkaloids including [[galantamine]], licensed for use against [[Alzheimer's disease]]. The alkaloids are bitter-tasting and toxic, and concentrated in the parts of the plant such as the stem most likely to be eaten by herbivores; they may also protect against [[parasite]]s.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bastida |first1=Jaume |last2=Lavilla |first2=Rodolfo |last3=Viladomat |first3=Francesc Viladomat |editor1-last=Cordell |editor1-first=G. A. |chapter=Chemical and Biological Aspects of ''Narcissus'' Alkaloids |date=2006 |volume=63 |pages=87–179 |doi=10.1016/S1099-4831(06)63003-4 |pmid=17133715 |title=The Alkaloids: Chemistry and Biology |pmc=7118783 |isbn=978-0-12-469563-4}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Galantamine |url=https://www.drugs.com/mtm/galantamine.html |publisher=Drugs.com |date=2017 |access-date=17 March 2018 |archive-date=14 October 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181014091614/https://www.drugs.com/mtm/galantamine.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |pmid=16437532 |year=2006 |last1=Birks |first1=J. |editor1-first=Jacqueline S |editor1-last=Birks |title=Cholinesterase inhibitors for Alzheimer's disease |journal=The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |volume=2016 |issue=1 |article-number=CD005593 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD005593|pmc=9006343 }}</ref>

Modern knowledge of medicinal plants is being systematised in the Medicinal Plant Transcriptomics Database, which by 2011 provided a sequence reference for the [[transcriptome]] of some thirty species.<ref name="danforth">{{cite web |title=Transcriptome Characterization, Sequencing, And Assembly Of Medicinal Plants Relevant To Human Health |url=http://apps.pharmacy.uic.edu/depts/pcrps/MedTranscriptomePlants/ |publisher=University of Illinois at Chicago |last=Soejarto |first=D. D. |date=1 March 2011 |access-date=26 January 2017 |archive-date=20 April 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170420235537/http://apps.pharmacy.uic.edu/depts/pcrps/MedTranscriptomePlants/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Major classes of plant [[phytochemical]]s are described below, with examples of plants that contain them.<ref name="Angio" /><ref name=Cravotto/><ref name="meskin-2002-p123">{{cite book |last=Meskin |first=Mark S. |title=Phytochemicals in Nutrition and Health |publisher=CRC Press|year=2002 |isbn=978-1-58716-083-7 |page=123 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cJHsMALUDj0C&pg=PA123}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Springbob |first1=Karen |last2=Kutchan |first2=Toni M. |chapter=Introduction to the different classes of natural products|editor=Lanzotti, Virginia |title=Plant-Derived Natural Products: Synthesis, Function, and Application |publisher=Springer |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-387-85497-7 |page=3 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Y8SpVXEng4QC&pg=PA3}}</ref><ref name="Elumalai">{{cite journal |last1=Elumalai |first1=A. |last2=Eswariah |first2=M. Chinna |title=Herbalism - A Review |journal=International Journal of Phytotherapy |date=2012 |volume=2 |issue=2 |pages=96–105 |url=http://www.phytotherapyjournal.com/File_Folder/96-105.pdf |access-date=2017-02-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170217232814/http://www.phytotherapyjournal.com/File_Folder/96-105.pdf |archive-date=2017-02-17 }}</ref>

===Alkaloids===

{{further|Alkaloids}}

[[Alkaloids]] are bitter-tasting chemicals, very widespread in nature, and often toxic, found in many medicinal plants.<ref name=Aniszewski2007>{{cite book |last=Aniszewski |first=Tadeusz |title=Alkaloids – secrets of life|location=Amsterdam |publisher=[[Elsevier]] |year=2007|isbn=978-0-444-52736-3 |page=182}}</ref> There are several classes with different modes of action as drugs, both recreational and pharmaceutical. Medicines of different classes include [[atropine]], [[scopolamine]], and [[hyoscyamine]] (all from [[nightshade]]),<ref name="EMEA">{{cite web |title=Atropa Belladonna |url=http://www.ema.europa.eu/docs/en_GB/document_library/Maximum_Residue_Limits_-_Report/2009/11/WC500010731.pdf |publisher=The European Agency for the Evaluation of Medicinal Products |access-date=26 February 2017 |date=1998 |archive-date=17 April 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180417200131/http://www.ema.europa.eu/docs/en_GB/document_library/Maximum_Residue_Limits_-_Report/2009/11/WC500010731.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> the traditional medicine [[berberine]] (from plants such as ''[[Berberis]]'' and ''[[Mahonia]]''),{{efn|Berberine is the main active component of an ancient Chinese herb ''Coptis chinensis'' French, which has been administered for what Yin and colleagues state is "[[diabetes]]" for thousands of years, although with no sound evidence of efficacy.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yin |first1=Jun |last2=Xing |first2=Huili |last3=Ye |first3=Jianping |title=Efficacy of Berberine in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes |journal=Metabolism |date=May 2008 |volume=57 |issue=5 |pages=712–717 |pmid=18442638 |pmc=2410097 |doi=10.1016/j.metabol.2008.01.013}}</ref>}} [[caffeine]] (''[[Coffea]]''), [[cocaine]] (''[[Coca]]''), [[ephedrine]] (''[[Ephedra (plant)|Ephedra]]''), morphine (opium poppy), [[nicotine]] ([[tobacco]]),{{efn|Tobacco has "probably been responsible for more deaths than any other herb", but it was used as a medicine in the societies encountered by Columbus and was considered a [[panacea]] in Europe. It is no longer accepted as medicinal.<ref name=Charlton2004>{{cite journal |last1=Charlton |first1=Anne |title=Medicinal uses of tobacco in history |journal=Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine|date=June 2004 |volume=97 |issue=6 |pages=292–296 |pmid=15173337 |doi=10.1177/014107680409700614 |pmc=1079499}}</ref>}} [[reserpine]] (''[[Rauvolfia serpentina]]''), [[quinidine]] and [[quinine]] (''[[Cinchona]]''), [[vincamine]] (''[[Vinca minor]]''), and [[vincristine]] (''[[Catharanthus roseus]]'').<ref name="Elumalai"/><ref name="Gremigni">{{cite journal |last1 =Gremigni|display-authors=etal|first1=P.|year=2003|title =The interaction of phosphorus and potassium with seed alkaloid concentrations, yield and mineral content in narrow-leafed lupin (Lupinus angustifolius L.) |journal=[[Plant and Soil]] |volume=253|issue=2 |pages =413–427 |jstor=24121197|doi=10.1023/A:1024828131581|bibcode=2003PlSoi.253..413G |s2cid=25434984}}</ref>

===Glycosides===

{{further|Glycosides}}

[[Anthraquinone]] [[glycosides]] are found in medicinal plants such as [[rhubarb]], [[Rhamnus purshiana|cascara]], and [[Alexandrian senna]]<!--aka Cassia senna, etc-->.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Zhe |author2=Ma, Pei |author3=He, Chunnian |author4=Peng, Yong |author5=Xiao, Peigen |title=Evaluation of the content variation of anthraquinone glycosides in rhubarb by UPLC-PDA |journal=Chemistry Central Journal |year=2013 |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=43–56 |doi=10.1186/1752-153X-7-170 |pmid=24160332 |pmc=3854541 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1016/S0378-6080(09)03148-1 |title=Treatments used in complementary and alternative medicine |volume=31 |pages=745–756 |series=Side Effects of Drugs Annual |year=2009 |last1=Chan |first1=K. |last2=Lin |first2=T.X. |isbn=978-0-444-53294-7 }}</ref> Plant-based [[laxative]]s made from such plants include [[senna (herb)|senna]],<ref name=Hietala>{{cite journal |last1=Hietala |first1=P. |author2=Marvola, M. |author3=Parviainen, T. |author4=Lainonen, H. |title=Laxative potency and acute toxicity of some anthraquinone derivatives, senna extracts and fractions of senna extracts |volume=61 |issue=2 |pages=153–156 |journal=Pharmacology & Toxicology |pmid=3671329 |date=August 1987 |doi=10.1111/j.1600-0773.1987.tb01794.x }}</ref> [[rhubarb]]<ref name=mehta>{{cite web |url=http://pharmaxchange.info/press/2012/12/pharmacognosy-of-rhubarb/ |title=Pharmacognosy of Rhubarb |last=Akolkar |first=Praful |work=PharmaXChange.info |date=2012-12-27 |access-date=2017-02-02 |archive-date=2015-06-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150626142055/http://pharmaxchange.info/press/2012/12/pharmacognosy-of-rhubarb/ |url-status=live }}</ref> and ''[[Aloe]]''.<ref name="Elumalai"/>

The [[cardiac glycoside]]s are powerful drugs from medicinal plants including [[foxglove]] and [[lily of the valley]]. They include [[digoxin]] and [[digitoxin]] which support the beating of the heart, and act as [[diuretic]]s.<ref name=USDAingredients>{{cite web |title=Active Plant Ingredients Used for Medicinal Purposes|url=https://www.fs.fed.us/wildflowers/ethnobotany/medicinal/ingredients.shtml |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture |access-date=18 February 2017 |quote=Below are several examples of active plant ingredients that provide medicinal plant uses for humans. |archive-date=12 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180712052048/https://www.fs.fed.us/wildflowers/ethnobotany/medicinal/ingredients.shtml |url-status=live}}</ref>

===Polyphenols===

{{further|Polyphenol|Health effects of polyphenols}}

[[Polyphenol]]s of several classes are widespread in plants, having diverse roles in defenses against plant diseases and predators.<ref name=USDAingredients/> They include hormone-mimicking [[phytoestrogen]]s and astringent [[tannin]]s.<ref name="Elumalai"/><ref name="Da Silva">{{cite journal |last1 =Da Silva|display-authors=etal|first1=Cecilia |year=2013|title =The High Polyphenol Content of Grapevine Cultivar Tannat Berries Is Conferred Primarily by Genes That Are Not Shared with the Reference Genome |journal=[[The Plant Cell]] |volume=25|issue=12 |pages=4777–4788 |jstor=43190600 |doi=10.1105/tpc.113.118810|pmid=24319081 |pmc=3903987 |bibcode=2013PlanC..25.4777D }}</ref> Plants containing phytoestrogens have been administered for centuries for [[gynecology|gynecological]] disorders, such as fertility, menstrual, and menopausal problems.<ref>{{cite book |last=Muller-Schwarze|first=Dietland |title=Chemical Ecology of Vertebrates |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2006|isbn=978-0-521-36377-8|page=287}}</ref> Among these plants are ''[[Pueraria]] mirifica'',<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=Y. S. |author2=Park J. S. |author3=Cho S. D. |author4=Son J. K. |author5=Cherdshewasart W. |author6=Kang K. S. |title=Requirement of metabolic activation for estrogenic activity of Pueraria mirifica |journal=Journal of Veterinary Science |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=273–277 |date=Dec 2002 |pmid=12819377 |url=http://www.koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO200210103477199.page |doi=10.4142/jvs.2002.3.4.273 |access-date=2019-04-19 |archive-date=2019-04-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190419160011/http://www.koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO200210103477199.page |url-status=live |doi-access=free }}</ref> [[kudzu]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Delmonte |first1=P. |author2=Rader, J. I. |title=Analysis of isoflavones in foods and dietary supplements |journal=Journal of AOAC International |volume=89 |issue=4 |pages=1138–46 |year=2006 |pmid=16915857 |doi= 10.1093/jaoac/89.4.1138|doi-access=free }}</ref> [[angelica]],<ref>{{cite book |first1=D.E. |last1=Brown|first2=N. J. |last2=Walton |title=Chemicals from Plants: Perspectives on Plant Secondary Products|publisher=World Scientific Publishing|year=1999|pages= 21, 141|isbn =978-981-02-2773-9}}</ref> [[fennel]], and [[anise]].<ref>{{cite journal |author=Albert-Puleo, M. |title=Fennel and anise as estrogenic agents |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |volume=2 |issue=4 |pages=337–44 |date=Dec 1980 |pmid=6999244 |doi=10.1016/S0378-8741(80)81015-4 }}</ref>

Many polyphenolic extracts, such as from [[grape seed]]s, [[olive]]s or [[pycnogenol|maritime pine bark]], are sold as [[dietary supplement]]s and [[cosmetics]] without proof or legal [[health claim]]s for medicinal effects.<ref name="efsa">{{cite journal |author=European Food Safety Authority |title=Scientific Opinion on the substantiation of health claims related to various food(s)/food constituent(s) and protection of cells from premature aging, antioxidant activity, antioxidant content and antioxidant properties, and protection of DNA, proteins and lipids from oxidative damage pursuant to Article 13(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/20061 |journal=EFSA Journal |year=2010 |volume=8 |issue=2 |page=1489 |doi=10.2903/j.efsa.2010.1489|doi-access=free }}</ref> In Ayurveda, the astringent rind of the [[pomegranate]], containing polyphenols called [[punicalagin]]s, is used as a medicine, with no scientific proof of efficacy.<ref name=efsa/><ref>{{cite book |title=Recent trends in horticulture in the Himalayas |last1=Jindal |first1=K. K. |author2=Sharma, R. C. |year=2004 |isbn=978-81-7387-162-7 |publisher=Indus Publishing |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LlogqveEFVgC}}</ref>

===Terpenes===

{{further|Terpenes}}

[[Terpenes]] and [[terpenoids]] of many kinds are found in a variety of medicinal plants,<ref>{{cite book |last=Wiart |first=Christopher |chapter=Terpenes |title=Lead Compounds from Medicinal Plants for the Treatment of Neurodegenerative Diseases |publisher=[[Elsevier]] |isbn=978-0-12-398373-2|doi= 10.1016/C2011-0-09611-4 |date=2014 |pages=189–284}}</ref> and in [[resin]]ous plants such as the [[conifers]]. They are strongly aromatic and serve to repel herbivores. Their scent makes them useful in [[essential oils]], whether for [[perfume]]s such as [[rose]] and [[lavender]], or for [[aromatherapy]].<ref name="Elumalai"/><ref name="tchen">{{cite journal |last1=Tchen |first1=T. T. |year=1965 |title=The Biosynthesis of Steroids, Terpenes and Acetogenins |journal=[[American Scientist]] |volume=53 |issue=4 |pages=499A–500A |jstor=27836252}}</ref><ref name="Singsaas">{{cite journal |last1=Singsaas|first1=Eric L.|year=2000 |title=Terpenes and the Thermotolerance of Photosynthesis |journal=[[New Phytologist]] |volume=146|issue=1 |pages=1–2 |jstor=2588737 |doi=10.1046/j.1469-8137.2000.00626.x|bibcode=2000NewPh.146....1S |doi-access=free }}</ref> Some have medicinal uses: for example, [[thymol]] is an antiseptic and was once used as a [[vermifuge]] (anti-worm medicine).<ref name=PubChemThymol/>

<gallery class="center" mode="nolines" widths="200px">
File:Thymian.jpg|The [[essential oil]] of [[common thyme]] (''Thymus vulgaris''), contains the [[monoterpene]] [[thymol]], an [[antiseptic]] and [[Antifungal medication|antifungal]].<ref name=PubChemThymol>{{cite web|title=Thymol (CID=6989)|url=https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/thymol|publisher=NIH|access-date=26 February 2017|quote=THYMOL is a phenol obtained from thyme oil or other volatile oils used as a stabilizer in pharmaceutical preparations, and as an antiseptic (antibacterial or antifungal) agent. It was formerly used as a vermifuge.|archive-date=12 July 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180712052716/https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/thymol|url-status=live}}</ref>
