Urban forestry has been shown to promote psychological healing, stress recovery, and to improve concentration and productivity.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shin |first1=Won Sop |last2=Yeoun |first2=Poung Sik |last3=Yoo |first3=Rhi Wha |last4=Shin |first4=Chang Seob |title=Forest experience and psychological health benefits: the state of the art and future prospect in Korea |journal=Environmental Health and Preventive Medicine |date=January 2010 |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=38–47 |doi=10.1007/s12199-009-0114-9 |pmid=19844774 |pmc=2793345 |bibcode=2010EHPM...15...38S }}</ref> [[Street tree]]s, if managed and cared for, are beneficial in creating sustainable and healthy communities.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Turner-Skoff|first1=J. |last2=Cavender|first2=N. |title=The Benefits of Trees for Livable and Sustainable Communities |journal=Plants, People, Planet |volume=1 |issue=4 |pages=323–335 |year=2019 |doi=10.1002/ppp3.39 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2019PlPP....1..323T }}</ref> The inequitable distribution of canopy cover in lower [[Socioeconomic status|socioeconomic]] neighborhoods has resulted in many social impacts that raise [[environmental justice]] concerns.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mills |first1=John R. |last2=Cunningham |first2=Patrick |last3=Donovan |first3=Geoffrey H. |date=2016 |title=Urban forests and social inequality in the Pacific Northwest |journal=Urban Forestry & Urban Greening |language=en |volume=16 |pages=188–196 |doi=10.1016/j.ufug.2016.02.011|doi-access=free |bibcode=2016UFUG...16..188M }}</ref>

{{toc limit|3}}

== Benefits ==
=== Environmental and health impacts ===
[[File:Midtown Sacramento Tree Canopy.jpg|thumb|Tree canopy over [[Midtown Sacramento]] suburban street]]
Heat waves cause 1,300 deaths each year in the United States alone, which is more than any other weather-related event.<ref name=":17">{{Cite web |last=Mcdonald |first=Rob |date=May 8, 2019 |title=Trees in the US Annually Prevent 1,200 Deaths During Heat Waves |url=https://blog.nature.org/science/2019/05/08/trees-in-the-us-annually-prevent-1200-deaths-during-heat-waves/ |website=Cool Green Science}}</ref> As temperatures continue to rise due to global warming, we can expect to see this number increasing in coming years. The risk is exacerbated for low-income households who do not have access to air conditioning, as well as heat-sensitive populations such as the elderly, infants, and those who have chronic health problems.

Reforesting a 10-meter radius corresponds to 0.7 degree Celsius decrease in daytime air temperature, compared to a 1.3 degree decrease in a 30-meter radius, and over 1.5 degrees in a 60 or 90 meter radius.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ziter |first1=Carly D. |last2=Pedersen |first2=Eric J. |last3=Kucharik |first3=Christopher J. |last4=Turner |first4=Monica G. |date=2019-03-25 |title=Scale-dependent interactions between tree canopy cover and impervious surfaces reduce daytime urban heat during summer |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=116 |issue=15 |pages=7575–7580 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1817561116 |pmid=30910972 |pmc=6462107 |bibcode=2019PNAS..116.7575Z |issn=0027-8424|doi-access=free }}</ref> This reduces the risk of [[heat stroke]], decreases cooling costs, and improves general well-being.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Zj88DgAAQBAJ&q=urban+forest+cultivating+green+infrastructure|title=The Urban Forest: Cultivating Green Infrastructure for People and the Environment|last1=Pearlmutter|first1=David|date=2017-02-27|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-3-319-50280-9|access-date=25 April 2018}}</ref>

Trees have saved 1,200 lives annually in the U.S., by preventing heat related deaths.<ref name=":17" /> Urban forests improve [[air quality]] by absorbing pollutants such as ozone, nitrogen dioxide, ammonia, and particulate matter as well as performing [[carbon sequestration]].<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=de-WvS5dlyEC&q=urban+forests+and+trees|title=Urban Forests and Trees: A Reference Book|last1=Konijnendijk|first1=Cecil C.|date=2005-05-20|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-3-540-25126-2|access-date=25 April 2018}}</ref> Communities with better air quality measures demonstrate lower levels of childhood asthma.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tiotiu |first1=Angelica I. |last2=Novakova |first2=Plamena |last3=Nedeva |first3=Denislava |last4=Chong-Neto |first4=Herberto Jose |last5=Novakova |first5=Silviya |last6=Steiropoulos |first6=Paschalis |last7=Kowal |first7=Krzysztof |date=September 2020 |title=Impact of Air Pollution on Asthma Outcomes |journal=International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health |volume=17 |issue=17 |page=6212 |doi=10.3390/ijerph17176212 |issn=1661-7827 |pmc=7503605 |pmid=32867076|doi-access=free }}</ref> Urban forestry can be an important tool for [[stormwater management]] as trees intercept rainwater in the canopy, and can slow down, filter and pump water back into the atmosphere via their roots.<ref name="storm2">{{cite web|url=http://water.epa.gov/polwaste/green/upload/stormwater2streettrees.pdf|title=Stormwater to Street Trees|website=United States Environmental Protection Agency|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150515235052/http://water.epa.gov/polwaste/green/upload/stormwater2streettrees.pdf|archive-date=2015-05-15|access-date=September 4, 2015|date=2015-04-24}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Berland |first1=Adam |last2=Shiflett |first2=Sheri A. |last3=Shuster |first3=William D. |last4=Garmestani |first4=Ahjond S. |last5=Goddard |first5=Haynes C. |last6=Herrmann |first6=Dustin L. |last7=Hopton |first7=Matthew E. |title=The role of trees in urban stormwater management |journal=Landscape and Urban Planning |date=June 2017 |volume=162 |pages=167–177 |doi=10.1016/j.landurbplan.2017.02.017|pmid=30220756 |pmc=6134866 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2017LUrbP.162..167B }}</ref> Other benefits include noise control, traffic control, and glare and reflection control.<ref>Kielbaso J.J. (2008) Management of Urban Forests in the United States. In: Carreiro M.M., Song YC., Wu J. (eds) Ecology, Planning, and Management of Urban Forests. Springer, New York, NY</ref>

=== Mental health impacts ===
[[File:Fairfield, New South Wales, Australia.jpg|thumb|A [[bird's-eye view]] image of [[Western Sydney]], Australia, showing the urban tree canopy]]
A 2018 study asked low income residents of [[Philadelphia]] "how often they felt nervous, hopeless, restless, depressed and worthless."<ref name="wapo20182">{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/inspired-life/wp/2018/08/17/study-when-a-citys-trashy-lots-are-cleaned-up-residents-mental-health-improves/|title=Study: When a city's trashy lots are cleaned up, residents' mental health improves|last=Hui|first=Mary|date=August 17, 2018|newspaper=Washington Post|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180817152402/https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/inspired-life/wp/2018/08/17/study-when-a-citys-trashy-lots-are-cleaned-up-residents-mental-health-improves/|archive-date=2018-08-17|url-status=live|access-date=2018-08-18}}</ref> As an experimental mental health intervention, trash was removed from vacant lots. Some of the vacant lots were "greened", with [[Tree planting|plantings of trees]], grass, and small fences. Residents near the "greened" lots who had incomes below the poverty line reported a decrease in feelings of depression of 68%, while residents with incomes above the poverty line reported a decrease of 41%. Removing trash from vacant lots without installing landscaping did not have an observable mental health impact.<ref name="wapo20182" />

Urban forests and green spaces have been associated with milder [[Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder|ADHD]] symptoms.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Faber Taylor |first1=Andrea |last2=Kuo |first2=Frances E. Ming |title=Could Exposure to Everyday Green Spaces Help Treat ADHD? Evidence from Children's Play Settings |journal=Applied Psychology: Health and Well-Being |date=November 2011 |volume=3 |issue=3 |pages=281–303 |doi=10.1111/j.1758-0854.2011.01052.x |doi-access=free }}</ref> Children with ADHD struggle with directed attention—a type of attention that is a part of the theory of attention restoration. Directed attention entails "periods of deliberate focus" and requires breaks to continue productivity.'''<ref>{{Cite web|date=2015-08-11|title=How Urban Forests Can Help Mitigate ADHD Symptoms|url=https://www.americanforests.org/blog/how-urban-forests-can-help-mitigate-adhd-symptoms/|access-date=2021-03-04|website=American Forests|language=en-US}}</ref>'''

A case study conducted in [[Belgrade]], Serbia, evaluated the mental health benefits of The Faculty Urban Forest for a younger population. Time spent in an arboretum is shown to benefit mental health by lowering [[Depression (mood)|depression]], anxiety, and stress.<ref name=":20">{{Cite journal |last1=Vujcic |first1=Maja |last2=Tomicevic-Dubljevic |first2=Jelena |date=2018-11-01 |title=Urban forest benefits to the younger population: The case study of the city of Belgrade, Serbia |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1389934117304008 |journal=Forest Policy and Economics |language=en |volume=96 |pages=54–62 |doi=10.1016/j.forpol.2018.08.006 |bibcode=2018ForPE..96...54V |s2cid=158968387 |issn=1389-9341|url-access=subscription }}</ref> An ideal forest environment for psychological improvement should have an extensive assortment of [[coniferous]] and [[broadleaved]] species displaying vibrant colors. These conditions provide a multitude of [[Sensory nervous system|sensory]] experiences, which can be experienced with infrastructure such as benches, picnic tables, and [[pavilion]]s.<ref name=":20" /> It is important to provide handicap-accessible options and locate urban forests close to public transportation so that they can support daily visits and restorative experiences for all.<ref name=":20" />

=== Tree canopy inequity ===
Urban tree canopy inequity is defined by [[American Forests]] as the uneven distribution of urban trees in neighborhoods that are socioeconomically disadvantaged.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tree Equity |url=https://www.americanforests.org/our-programs/tree-equity/ |access-date=2022-04-29 |website=American Forests |language=en-US}}</ref>  These neighborhoods that lack sufficient canopy cover compared to areas that have access to suitable canopy cover, experience inaccessibility to the benefits that trees provide, and other social inequalities.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jenerette |first1=G. Darrel |last2=Harlan |first2=Sharon L. |last3=Stefanov |first3=William L. |last4=Martin |first4=Chris A. |date=October 2011 |title=Ecosystem services and urban heat riskscape moderation: water, green spaces, and social inequality in Phoenix, USA |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1890/10-1493.1 |journal=Ecological Applications |language=en |volume=21 |issue=7 |pages=2637–2651 |doi=10.1890/10-1493.1 |pmid=22073649 |bibcode=2011EcoAp..21.2637J |hdl=2286/R.I.55218 |s2cid=8315579 |issn=1051-0761|hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Many of the neighborhoods that are most impacted by this inequity are where minorities and impoverished populations reside.  This inequity of the urban tree canopy is caused by many social factors, such as [[environmental racism]], which is environmental injustice that largely impacts racial groups by policies or practices, such as [[redlining]] policies. This resulted in the trend that poorer and predominantly minority neighborhoods experience less canopy cover.

Urban tree canopy inequity limits the access to the beneficial ecosystem services that trees provide.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fan |first1=Chao |last2=Johnston |first2=Mark |last3=Darling |first3=Lindsay |last4=Scott |first4=Lydia |last5=Liao |first5=Felix Haifeng |date=January 2019 |title=Land use and socio-economic determinants of urban forest structure and diversity |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0169204618309885 |journal=Landscape and Urban Planning |language=en |volume=181 |pages=10–21 |doi=10.1016/j.landurbplan.2018.09.012|bibcode=2019LUrbP.181...10F |s2cid=92276115 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>  Populations that do not live in neighborhoods with suitable canopy cover do not experience the protection from the impacts of [[climate change]] and the [[Urban heat island|urban heat island effect]], air and water pollution, trapping of rainfall surface runoff, and energy savings on air conditioning from tree shade. These populations also do not benefit from the psychological benefits that trees provide, such as having areas that increase social cohesion and congregation, recreation, and nature aesthetics.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nowak |first1=David J. |last2=Hirabayashi |first2=Satoshi |last3=Bodine |first3=Allison |last4=Greenfield |first4=Eric |date=2014-10-01 |title=Tree and forest effects on air quality and human health in the United States |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0269749114002395 |journal=Environmental Pollution |language=en |volume=193 |pages=119–129 |doi=10.1016/j.envpol.2014.05.028 |pmid=25016465 |bibcode=2014EPoll.193..119N |issn=0269-7491|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

An example of other social benefits associated with urban tree canopy includes a research study reviewed by [[Children & Nature Network|The Children & Nature Network]], an organization active in the movement of connecting children and their families to nature. Researchers conclude that there is a positive relationship between academic performance and tree cover and [[Species richness|species composition]], indicating that tree cover and species composition have a positive effect on the academic performance of primary school-aged children, especially those enrolled in socio-economically challenged schools.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tree cover and species composition have a positive effect on children's academic performance, especially for children in socio-economically challenged schools |url=https://research.childrenandnature.org/research/tree-cover-and-species-composition-have-a-positive-effect-on-childrens-academic-performance-especially-for-children-in-socio-economically-challenged-schools/ |access-date=2022-04-29 |website=Children and Nature Network |language=en}}</ref>

[[File:In the shade of plane trees, north side of Marylebone Road, nearing Baker Street - geograph.org.uk - 4105143 (cropped).jpg|thumb|upright|Pedestrians walking in the shade of mature [[London plane|plane trees]] on a hot August day in central London]]
A lack of trees in neighborhoods and a heavy presence of [[impervious surface]]s such as houses, sidewalks, and parking lots, contribute to the heat island effect and there is a lack of temperature moderation. In these areas, temperatures are more extreme.  Without the presence of trees, there would be poor air quality and an increase in [[air pollution]] as trees remove carbon and pollutants from the air through [[Carbon sequestration|sequestration]], and storing it in their structures. A lack of trees would also result in the risk of chemicals and other harmful pollutants entering water sources and collecting on sidewalks and roads, as they would not be present to increase [[Infiltration (hydrology)|infiltration]] and to help reduce and manage [[Surface runoff|rainwater runoff]]. [[Biodiversity]] and [[habitat]] for animals decline in these areas as trees are not available for animals and plants to utilize.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Riley |first1=Christopher B. |last2=Gardiner |first2=Mary M. |date=2020-02-11 |title=Examining the distributional equity of urban tree canopy cover and ecosystem services across United States cities |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=15 |issue=2 |article-number=e0228499 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0228499 |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=7012407 |pmid=32045427|bibcode=2020PLoSO..1528499R |doi-access=free }}</ref>

As urban tree canopy inequity remains present in lower-socioeconomically disadvantaged neighborhoods, impacting the livelihoods and environmental state of these areas and populations, efforts are being made by urban foresters, city officials, and organizations to address this problem and present solutions.  Examples of these efforts include the [[United States Forest Service]] outreach and education programs.  Organizations such as [[Casey Trees|Casey Tree's]] Community Tree Planting projects, the [[The Greening of Detroit|Greening of Detroit]] program, and [[American Forests]] help to implement programs and initiatives within cities and neighborhoods to engage volunteers, preserve and care for the urban forest and promote educational and career opportunities for the public.

[[Case study|Case studies]], such as one based in [[Washington, D.C.|Washington, D.C]]., analyze and contribute to the knowledge of urban tree canopy inequity by utilizing various methods including interviews, collaboration with private and public organizations, and [[Outreach|community outreach]] that are successful and help present solutions for urban tree canopy inequity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Leets |first1=Laura |last2=Sprenger |first2=Amber |last3=Hartman |first3=Robert O. |last4=Howard Jackson |first4=Jessica |last5=Britt |first5=Marge |last6=Gulley |first6=Andrew |last7=Simon Thomas |first7=Juli |last8=Wijesinghe |first8=Sanith |date=2022-03-01 |title=Promoting tree equity in Washington, D.C. |journal=Trees, Forests and People |language=en |volume=7 |article-number=100209 |doi=10.1016/j.tfp.2022.100209 |s2cid=246581928 |issn=2666-7193|doi-access=free |bibcode=2022TFP.....700209L }}</ref> The use of online applications such as [[i-Tree]] and its associated tree and forest assessment tools, and Tree Equity Score,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tree Equity Score |url=https://treeequityscore.org/ |access-date=2022-04-29 |website=treeequityscore.org |language=en}}</ref> along with many others, assist urban foresters, professionals, and students in conducting research on urban areas and presenting planning solutions to urban tree canopy inequity.

==== Inequities in environmental and health impacts ====
In the 1930s as part of the [[New Deal]], the federal government started implementing unfair [[redlining]] policies, which classified certain neighborhoods as "risky" areas for banks and mortgage lenders to approve in funding home investments. Demographics of these communities typically included higher percentages of Black, African American, and Latino community members. These [[redlining]] policies led to overall lack in investment in these areas, including lack of equitable investment in environmental resources.<ref name=":10">{{Cite web |last=Treglia |first=M |title=The State of the Urban Forest in New York City |url=https://www.nature.org/content/dam/tnc/nature/en/photos/TheStateoftheNYCUrbanForest.pdf |website=The Nature Conservancy |access-date=2022-04-03 |archive-date=2022-06-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220615164715/https://www.nature.org/content/dam/tnc/nature/en/photos/TheStateoftheNYCUrbanForest.pdf }}</ref> There remain lower percentages of [[Canopy (biology)|tree canopy]] coverage in nearly every U.S. city that had formerly redlined neighborhoods, including the three most populous U.S. cities, [[New York City|New York]], [[Chicago]], and [[Los Angeles]].<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Plumer |first1=Brad |last2=Popovich |first2=Nadja |last3=Palmer |first3=Brian |date=2020-08-24 |title=How Decades of Racist Housing Policy Left Neighborhoods Sweltering |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2020/08/24/climate/racism-redlining-cities-global-warming.html |access-date=2022-04-03 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=Racist Housing Practices From The 1930s Linked To Hotter Neighborhoods Today |language=en |work=NPR.org |url=https://www.npr.org/2020/01/14/795961381/racist-housing-practices-from-the-1930s-linked-to-hotter-neighborhoods-today |access-date=2022-04-03}}</ref> People living in urban communities with significantly lower percentages of urban trees do not benefit from the same environmental and health impacts as those in communities with greater tree populations.

In New York, specifically, the [[South Bronx]] has far fewer trees than New York City neighborhoods with higher income levels. Tree canopy coverage in the [[The Bronx|Bronx]], in general, is the lowest of all five New York City boroughs. There is only 19.86% canopy coverage provided by street trees, which is much lower than the citywide average of 23.98%. The [[New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene|New York City Department of Health's]] [https://a816-dohbesp.nyc.gov/IndicatorPublic/VisualizationData.aspx?id=2191,4466a0,100,Summarize Heat Vulnerability Index (HVI)] measures how the risk of heat related illness and death differs across city neighborhoods, and it shows that New York City neighborhoods that are more heat-vulnerable, such as those in the South Bronx, tend to have lower tree canopy coverage.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The New York City Department of Health, Heat Vulnerability Index |url=https://a816-dohbesp.nyc.gov/IndicatorPublic/VisualizationData.aspx?id=2191,4466a0,100,Summarize}}</ref> 

Populations living in these communities are at greater risk for heat related illness, such as [[heat stroke]], or death due to [[heat wave]]s. Health outcomes associated with [[air pollution]], such as [[asthma]], are also worse off in neighborhoods with lower tree canopy coverage.<ref name=":10" /> In the Bronx, childhood asthma rates are disproportionately high. Children in the Bronx visit the emergency room for asthma 2x the rate of children in other boroughs. There are approximately 17% of children (age 13 and younger) suffering from asthma in the Bronx, compared to the citywide average of 11%.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Disparities among Children with Asthma in New York City |url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/epi/databrief126.pdf |website=The New York City Department of Health}}</ref>

=== Impacts on wildlife ===
[[File:Birds nests in Trees, Lovers Lane, Thurso - geograph.org.uk - 1204802.jpg|thumb|Birds' nests in trees]]

Urban forests in the built environment affect [[urban wildlife]] in several ways. An urban habitat can impact wildlife behavior significantly and can alter the ecology of urban wildlife, influencing these organisms' behavior. The interactions between humans and wildlife and the impacts of urbanization on these wildlife populations influence cities across the world.

==== Disturbances ====
[[Disturbance (ecology)|Disturbance]]s in urban forests are known for occurring more frequently and with higher intensities than in nature. Changes in the [[urban landscape]] can lead to greater [[Competition (biology)|competition]] for resources among species on fragmented areas of land, leading to more stress for urban wildlife.<ref name=":03">{{cite journal |last1=Murray |first1=Maureen H |last2=Sánchez |first2=Cecilia A |last3=Becker |first3=Daniel J |last4=Byers |first4=Kaylee A |last5=Worsley-Tonks |first5=Katherine EL |last6=Craft |first6=Meggan E |title=City sicker? A meta-analysis of wildlife health and urbanization |journal=Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment |date=December 2019 |volume=17 |issue=10 |pages=575–583 |doi=10.1002/fee.2126 |bibcode=2019FrEE...17..575M |s2cid=209585355 }}</ref> Urban wildlife is also exposed to warmer temperatures as well as higher levels of pollution as cities alter the natural environment significantly.<ref name=":03" />

The construction of [[urban infrastructure]] requires [[deforestation]], leveling, and other activities that lead to [[habitat fragmentation]], reduced [[genetic diversity]], and changes in behavior.<ref name=":22">{{cite journal |last1=Referowska-Chodak |first1=Ewa |title=Pressures and Threats to Nature Related to Human Activities in European Urban and Suburban Forests |journal=Forests |date=4 September 2019 |volume=10 |issue=9 |page=765 |doi=10.3390/f10090765 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2019Fore...10..765R }}</ref> Urban wildlife is also exposed to higher amounts of toxic substances, including [[heavy metals]], road treatments, or [[pesticide]]s from lawns that can lead to abnormal reproduction or development.<ref name=":03" /> Consumption of prey species by domesticated pets, such as dogs and cats, also leads to an increased mortality rate in urban habitats.<ref name=":22" /> Urban forests are essential to creating habitats for wildlife within cities, and many species have adapted to living in the disturbed conditions of the built environment by utilizing urban green-spaces.<ref name=":32">{{Cite journal|last=Dunster|first=J. A.|date=May 1998|title=The role of arborists in providing wildlife habitat and landscape linkages throughout the urban forest |journal=Journal of Arboriculture |volume=24 |issue=3 |url=https://treecareforbirds.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/The-Role-of-Arborists-in-Providing-Wildlife-Habitat-and-Landscape-Linkages-Throughout-the-Urban-Forest-Dunster-1998.pdf |via=Tree Care for Birds}}</ref> Research has shown diverse green-spaces to be better suited for wildlife. For example, in [[Kraków]], Poland, the species richness of owls was higher in parts of the city with varied land uses than more homogeneous areas.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fröhlich |first1=Arkadiusz |last2=Ciach |first2=Michał |title=Nocturnal noise and habitat homogeneity limit species richness of owls in an urban environment |journal=Environmental Science and Pollution Research |date=June 2019 |volume=26 |issue=17 |pages=17284–17291 |doi=10.1007/s11356-019-05063-8 |pmid=31012067 |pmc=6546646 |bibcode=2019ESPR...2617284F }}</ref> Additional support for land-use diversity in urban areas is provided in a study showing the importance of leaving dead and decaying trees on the landscape for wildlife habitat.<ref name=":32" />

Urban forests can alter natural diets by providing [[dietary supplement]]s to wildlife in the form of fruit or nut-producing ornamental plants, trash, or even domestic pets like cats.<ref name=":13">{{cite journal |last1=Larson |first1=Rachel N. |last2=Brown |first2=Justin L. |last3=Karels |first3=Tim |last4=Riley |first4=Seth P. D. |title=Effects of urbanization on resource use and individual specialization in coyotes (Canis latrans) in southern California |journal=PLOS ONE |date=5 February 2020 |volume=15 |issue=2 |article-number=e0228881 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0228881 |pmid=32023321 |pmc=7001990 |bibcode=2020PLoSO..1528881L |doi-access=free }}</ref> By examining [[coyote]] scat and using stable isotope analysis, it was estimated that about 22% of the scat or 38% of the urban coyote diet was from human-created sources.<ref name=":13" />

Having wildlife interacting around humans in urban areas can create conflicts between humans and animals. A case study in [[Aspen, Colorado]] observed the foraging habits of bears, tracking their movements using [[GPS collar]]s, and found that bears visited forested areas in the city with fruit-bearing trees for food.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lewis |first1=D. L. |last2=Baruch-Mordo |first2=S. |last3=Wilson |first3=K. R. |last4=Breck |first4=S. W. |last5=Mao |first5=J. S. |last6=Broderick |first6=J. |title=Foraging ecology of black bears in urban environments: guidance for human-bear conflict mitigation |journal=Ecosphere |date=August 2015 |volume=6 |issue=8 |pages=art141 |doi=10.1890/ES15-00137.1 |doi-access=free |hdl=10217/169978 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Alternatively, in a study on the [[behavioral ecology]] of urban deer populations, the authors discussed the difficulty of managing this species due to its positive public perception as an aesthetically pleasing animal.<ref name=":4">{{cite journal |last1=Honda |first1=T. |last2=Iijima |first2=H. |last3=Tsuboi |first3=J. |last4=Uchida |first4=K. |title=A review of urban wildlife management from the animal personality perspective: The case of urban deer |journal=Science of the Total Environment |date=December 2018 |volume=644 |pages=576–582 |doi=10.1016/j.scitotenv.2018.06.335 |pmid=29990907 |bibcode=2018ScTEn.644..576H |s2cid=51621354 }}</ref> Proper species selection, placement of trees, and other urban forest management strategies can be utilized to mitigate human-wildlife conflicts in cities.<ref name=":4" />

===Ecosystem services===
{{see also|Ecosystem service}}

==== Cultural services ====
Cultural services are non-material benefits (such as aesthetics and spiritual enrichment) that can be obtained from an ecosystem.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Endreny |first1=Theodore A. |title=Strategically growing the urban forest will improve our world |journal=Nature Communications |date=December 2018 |volume=9 |issue=1 |article-number=1160 |doi=10.1038/s41467-018-03622-0  |doi-access=free|pmid=29563541 |pmc=5862988 |bibcode=2018NatCo...9.1160E }}</ref> Certain tree species have cultural value to different groups of people, and different tree species provide a range of different aesthetic values. The tree species that urban foresters plant affect many cultural benefits provided by urban forestry, such as an increase in physical health, psychological health, social health, property values, [[community economic development]], and tourism.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nesbitt |first1=Lorien |last2=Hotte |first2=Ngaio |last3=Barron |first3=Sara |last4=Cowan |first4=Judith |last5=Sheppard |first5=Stephen R.J. |title=The social and economic value of cultural ecosystem services provided by urban forests in North America: A review and suggestions for future research |journal=Urban Forestry & Urban Greening |date=July 2017 |volume=25 |pages=103–111 |doi=10.1016/j.ufug.2017.05.005 |bibcode=2017UFUG...25..103N }}</ref> Understanding the values and interests of the different stakeholders in the community can help improve the cultural services provided through urban forestry.

==== Regulating services ====
Trees are important in regulating ecosystem processes; they contribute to filtering air pollution, microclimate regulation, carbon dioxide sequestration, and reducing climate change.<ref name="Solomou et al 2018">{{cite journal |last1=Solomou |first1=Alexandra D. |last2=Topalidou |first2=Eleni T. |last3=Germani |first3=Rafaelia |last4=Argiri |first4=Apostolia |last5=Karetsos |first5=George |title=Importance, Utilization and Health of Urban Forests: A Review |journal=Notulae Botanicae Horti Agrobotanici Cluj-Napoca |date=27 November 2018 |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=10–16 |doi=10.15835/nbha47111316 |bibcode=2018NBHAC..47...10S |s2cid=91632390 |doi-access=free |hdl=11615/79186 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Trees can reduce the urban heat island effect through shading paved areas, aiding in airflow, and [[evapotranspiration]]. When planted and managed properly, these cooling benefits extend past the city itself.<ref name="Solomou et al 2018"/>

If not planted in locations ideal for their survival, trees will be vulnerable to disease. Diseased trees provide decreased ecosystem services, making it important for urban forestry to be a part of the planning and management of the urban canopy. Trees in urban environments can also aid in stormwater management and reduce the risk of flash floods by intercepting rainfall in the tree canopy. Tree canopy interception can also minimize the amount of sediment and nutrient contamination that occurs downstream.<ref name=":35">{{cite journal |last1=Matteo |first1=Michelle |last2=Randhir |first2=Timothy |last3=Bloniarz |first3=David |title=Watershed-Scale Impacts of Forest Buffers on Water Quality and Runoff in Urbanizing Environment |journal=Journal of Water Resources Planning and Management |date=May 2006 |volume=132 |issue=3 |pages=144–152 |doi=10.1061/(ASCE)0733-9496(2006)132:3(144) }}</ref> This is now a focus in cities around the world through using water sensitive urban design (WSUD) in urban forestry.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Livesley |first1=S. J. |last2=McPherson |first2=E. G. |last3=Calfapietra |first3=C. |title=The Urban Forest and Ecosystem Services: Impacts on Urban Water, Heat, and Pollution Cycles at the Tree, Street, and City Scale |journal=Journal of Environmental Quality |date=January 2016 |volume=45 |issue=1 |pages=119–124 |doi=10.2134/jeq2015.11.0567 |pmid=26828167 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2016JEnvQ..45..119L }}</ref> Urban forests protect watershed health by utilizing riparian and street buffering with urban forestry practices.<ref name=":35" />

==== Provisioning services ====
[[File:2008-04-21 Tree trimming on Gregson St 1.jpg|thumb|Tree pruning in [[Durham, North Carolina]].]]
There are many different tree species that provide provisioning services in the urban forest. These services have a variety of names, including [[urban agriculture]] and edible green infrastructure.<ref name=":16">{{cite journal |last1=Russo |first1=Alessio |last2=Escobedo |first2=Francisco J. |last3=Cirella |first3=Giuseppe T. |last4=Zerbe |first4=Stefan |title=Edible green infrastructure: An approach and review of provisioning ecosystem services and disservices in urban environments |journal=Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment |date=May 2017 |volume=242 |pages=53–66 |doi=10.1016/j.agee.2017.03.026 |bibcode=2017AgEE..242...53R |s2cid=90554248 |url=http://eprints.glos.ac.uk/6587/9/6588%20Russo%20Edible%20green%20infrastructure.pdf }}</ref> Wild food products produced from trees pose a variety of benefits to the residents in that area. They can supply food to local residents and wildlife and increase biodiversity in the community. These trees can be harvested by local residents with minimal education on urban foraging. Some examples of urban agriculture are fruit trees and rooftop gardens. While fruit trees can provide produce and many other benefits, they can also create a mess if the produce is not harvested and fruit is left on the ground.

Proper [[pruning]] can help reduce the mess created but not eliminate it. An urban forest that can provide produce significantly cuts down on food transportation from distant farms and therefore lowers carbon emissions annually.<ref name=":16" /> Urban wood utilization is an often overlooked provisioning service. Almost 70% of urban wood is wasted while only 25% is recycled and/or reused.<ref name=":25">{{cite web |last1=Bratkovich |first1=Steve |last2=Bowyer |first2=Jim |last3=Fernholz |first3=Kathryn |last4=Lindburg |first4=Alison |title=Urban tree utilization and why it matters |date=23 January 2008 |url=https://www.dovetailinc.org/report_pdfs/2008/dovetailurban0108ig.pdf }}</ref> Urban wood that is reused can be turned into useful products, such as furniture or [[bioenergy]].<ref name=":25" />

==== Supporting services ====
The supporting ecosystem services are necessary for the production of all other ecosystem services. Some of these services include biomass production, [[nutrient cycling]], [[Pedogenesis|soil formation]], and biodiversity. Additionally, proper management of urban forests can provide habits for native wildlife, including endangered species.<ref name="Solomou et al 2018"/> Urban forests that include a large range of native and exotic trees provide a large range of habitats for wildlife. It has been shown in Sweden that certain endangered bird species mainly inhabit urban forests where certain trees are planted. One Swedish city contains two thirds of the red-list endangered species of the area by including endangered plants and habitats for endangered wildlife.<ref name="Solomou et al 2018"/>

== Wildlife habitat management ==
[[File:ISA Certified Municipal Arborist, James Kinder.jpg|right|thumb|James Kinder, an [[International Society of Arboriculture|ISA]] Certified Municipal [[Arborist]] examining a Japanese Hemlock at [[Hoyt Arboretum]].]]
The urban forest provides habitat for many wildlife species, including song birds, squirrels and other small mammals, and insects.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Urban Wildlife Basics|url=http://urbanwildlifegroup.org/urban-wildlife-information|access-date=2021-04-13|website=The Urban Wildlife Working Group|language=en-US}}</ref> The urban forest provides the basics that animals need for survival; food, water, shelter, and space or habitat. [[Fruit]] or [[Mast (botany)|mast]] producing trees provide food sources, trees and other vegetation provide shelter and habitats, and artificial water sources in cities and their parks provide water.<ref name=":06">{{Cite web|last=Cecil|first=Kyle|title=Urban Wildlife: Challenges and Opportunities - Other Resources - Local Community Resources - University of Illinois Extension|url=https://web.extension.illinois.edu/lcr/wildlife.cfm|access-date=2021-04-13|website=web.extension.illinois.edu}}</ref> The urban forest can be planned and managed in the context of the wildlife populations in the area, increasing the population of desired species or decreasing the population of undesirable or invasive ones based on the biological and/or cultural [[carrying capacity]] of the municipality.

=== Biodiversity and threatened/endangered species ===
[[Biodiversity]] has been declining across the world due to [[climate change]], [[deforestation]], and the destruction of [[critical habitat]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Martin|title=UN Report: Nature's Dangerous Decline 'Unprecedented'; Species Extinction Rates 'Accelerating'|url=https://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/blog/2019/05/nature-decline-unprecedented-report|access-date=2021-05-02|website=United Nations Sustainable Development|date=6 May 2019 |language=en-US}}</ref> Preserving and bolstering biodiversity ensures that ecosystems of all kinds are functioning properly, and we can thus reap the benefits of [[Ecosystem service|ecosystem services]]. [[Urbanization]] holds potential solutions to achieve high levels of biodiversity when managed correctly. In the United States, the [[Endangered Species Act of 1973|Endangered Species Act's]] language acts as a means to protect not only listed species but also the conservation of their habitats to sustain them, many of which are found in urban areas. Multiple transcontinental research projects on urban wildlife have found that there is a consistent positive correlation between human [[population density]] and [[species richness]] across all vertebrate [[Taxonomy (biology)|taxonomic groups]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alvey |first1=Alexis A. |title=Promoting and preserving biodiversity in the urban forest |journal=Urban Forestry & Urban Greening |date=December 2006 |volume=5 |issue=4 |pages=195–201 |doi=10.1016/j.ufug.2006.09.003 |bibcode=2006UFUG....5..195A }}</ref>

Urban areas provide and maintain a mosaic of diverse wildlife habitat to support existing and introduced fauna. Urban Forestry Management Plans in conjunction with Wildlife Management Plans can support and improve urban biodiversity by including following attributes: routine tree inventories to identify a biodiversity baseline for goal setting, intentional [[tree planting]] of hardy species to promote biodiversity, and lastly to focus on the preservation and improvement of [[urban park]]s and [[woodlot]]s as vital wooded and [[Edge effects|edge habitats]]. Challenges to managing for biodiversity and endangered species include the difficulties in creating and managing artificial, fragmented, yet diverse habitat types simultaneously in the context of social problems such as poverty and crime.

=== Undesirable and invasive species ===
[[Invasive species]] are nonnative plants, animals, microbial pathogens, and fungi that cause damage environmentally and/or economically.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Invasive Species|url=https://www.fs.fed.us/foresthealth/protecting-forest/invasive-species/|access-date=2021-04-13|website=www.fs.fed.us}}</ref> These species are having a number of  negative effects on our forests, both wild and urban, from being a nuisance to compromising and killing native trees. Oftentimes, invasive species are introduced via urban areas that serve as [[Transport hub|transportation hubs]], meaning that the urban forest is typically the first to be affected by them, and can also serve as the first line of defense to keep them from invading native forests. Without one of the basics of survival, undesirable wildlife cannot inhabit the area. Trees and vegetation can be altered to decrease habitat space and fewer fruit producing trees could be planted or fruit could be cleaned up to limit food sources.<ref name=":06" />

In response to the growing prevalence, many municipalities have begun planting disease and pest resistant [[cultivar]]s, such as modified [[Ulmus americana|American elms]]<ref>{{Cite web|title=Restoring American Elms to their Native Range- Partnerships - Northern Research Station - USDA Forest Service|url=https://www.nrs.fs.fed.us/partners/elm/|access-date=2021-04-13|website=www.nrs.fs.fed.us|archive-date=2021-04-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210414210437/https://www.nrs.fs.fed.us/partners/elm/|url-status=dead}}</ref> and [[Fraxinus|ash trees]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jepson |first1=Paul R |last2=Arakelyan |first2=Irina |title=Developing publicly acceptable tree health policy: public perceptions of tree-breeding solutions to ash dieback among interested publics in the UK |journal=Forest Policy and Economics |date=July 2017 |volume=80 |pages=167–177 |doi=10.1016/j.forpol.2017.03.002 |pmid=28674479 |pmc=5473346 |bibcode=2017ForPE..80..167J }}</ref> to prevent the spread of the fungal [[Dutch elm disease]] and [[emerald ash borer]] infestations, respectively. There are also rising regulations against the planting of invasive tree species that are harmful to the naturally occurring ecosystems because they can out compete native species for resources or attract undesirable wildlife.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Purcell|first=Lindsey A.|title=Invasive Plant Species in our Urban Areas|url=https://extension.purdue.edu/article/24275|access-date=2021-04-13|website=extension.purdue.edu|language=en}}</ref> In April 2019, the state of Indiana enacted the Terrestrial Plants Rule,<ref>{{Cite web|last=DNR|date=2021-01-29|title=Terrestrial Invasive Species - Plants|url=https://www.in.gov/dnr/rules-and-regulations/invasive-species/terrestrial-invasive-species-plants/|access-date=2021-04-13|website=DNR|language=en}}</ref> banning 44 invasive nursery species that cause harm to the urban forest and attract undesirable wildlife, including [[Ailanthus altissima|tree-of-heaven]], [[honeysuckle]] and [[Elaeagnus umbellata|autumn olive]]. The [[Pyrus calleryana|Bradford pear]], a common landscape tree, has been banned from the state of [[Ohio]], and the cities of [[Charlotte, North Carolina]]<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Infamous Bradford Pear|url=https://franklin.ces.ncsu.edu/2019/03/the-infamous-bradford-pear-2/|access-date=2021-04-13|website=franklin.ces.ncsu.edu|date=6 March 2019 |language=en}}</ref> and [[Pittsburgh|Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=Pittsburgh Urban Forest Master Plan|url=https://www.treepittsburgh.org/resource/pittsburgh-urban-forest-master-plan/|access-date=2021-04-13|website=Tree Pittsburgh|language=en-US}}</ref> as they are known to spread quickly, [[Competitive exclusion principle|crowding out]] native vegetation types from [[grasses]] to [[hardwood]] trees, further fragmenting and damaging the habitat of native animals as well.

=== Social impact ===
Urban forest related events such as [[Tree planting|planting]] festivals can significantly reduce social isolation problems, enhance people's experience and raise environmental awareness. Urban forests also encourage more active lifestyles by providing space for exercise and are associated with reduced stress and overall emotional well-being. Urban forests may also provide products such as timber or food, and deliver economic benefits such as increased property values and the attraction of tourism, businesses and investment.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fao.org/3/a-i6210e.pdf|title=Guidelines on urban and peri-urban forestry|last1=Salbitano|first1=Fabio|publisher=Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180107171749/http://www.fao.org/3/a-i6210e.pdf|archive-date=2018-01-07|url-status=live|access-date=25 April 2018}}</ref>

==== Case study ====
The [[Denver|City of Denver]] Department of Parks and Recreation website<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://app.powerbigov.us/view?r=eyJrIjoiZjZiNGQ2NzctYmQ0MS00ZDlhLWJmMmUtNmM2MDM5MDc4N2RhIiwidCI6IjM5Yzg3YWIzLTY2MTItNDJjMC05NjIwLWE2OTZkMTJkZjgwMyJ9|title=Power BI Report|access-date=2018-06-01|language=en-US}}</ref> hosts interactive online tools that allow residents to view the financial impact to their neighborhoods directly related to healthy [[tree planting]]. In the Washington-Virginia Vale neighborhood the city website cites 2,002 individual trees as having been planted and maintained by the City Forester. These trees are believed to bring in an annual ecosystem benefit of $159,521. This is mostly wrapped up in property benefits, which cite a contribution to this total of $143,331. The majorities of these trees are between 0 and 12 feet tall and are a mix of mostly Elm, Maple, Pine, and Locust species.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.denvergov.org/content/denvergov/en/denver-parks-and-recreation/trees-natural-resources/forestry-trees-.html|title=Forestry (Trees)|website=City of Denver Parks and Recreation (Forestry)|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180422083003/http://www.denvergov.org/content/denvergov/en/denver-parks-and-recreation/trees-natural-resources/forestry-trees-.html|archive-date=2018-04-22|url-status=live|access-date=May 31, 2018}}</ref>

=== Economic impacts ===

==== Lifespan value ====
Trees serve an economical function within the urban forest, providing various monetary benefits. It is estimated that there are around 3.8 billion trees in urban areas around the United States, equating to $2.4 trillion in overall structural value.<ref name=":05">{{cite report |last1=Nowak |first1=David J. |last2=Stein |first2=Susan M. |last3=Randler |first3=Paula B. |last4=Greenfield |first4=Eric J. |last5=Comas |first5=Sara J. |last6=Carr |first6=Mary A. |last7=Alig |first7=Ralph J. |date=2010 |title=Sustaining America's urban trees and forests: a Forests on the Edge report |location=Newtown Square, PA |doi=10.2737/nrs-gtr-62 |doi-access=free}}</ref> In addition, environmental and social benefits such as air quality, climate change, water flow, real estate, and even community well-being can be quantified to determine their economical impact.<ref name=":05" /> Examples of the economic values created by the urban forest includes an annual $4.7 billion of air pollution removal, $3.8 billion in carbon sequestration.<ref name=":05" /> Additionally, recreational experiences have the potential to surpass $2 billion in annual value.<ref>{{cite web|title=Assessing the sustainability of agricultural and urban forests in the United States |url=https://www.fs.fed.us/nrs/pubs/jrnl/2016/nrs_2016_nowak_002.pdf|last=Nowak|first=D. J.|date=2016|website=United States Department of Agriculture, Forest Service. Chapter 4.}}</ref>

The value of an urban forest is estimated by quantifying social and ecosystem services, then assigning those services monetary worth, which are often based on market value.<ref name=":34">{{Citation |author=David J. Nowak |chapter=Assessing the benefits and economic values of trees |date=2017 |editor=Francesco Ferrini |editor2=Cecil C. Konijnendijk van den Bosch |editor3=Alessio Fini |title=Routledge Handbook of Urban Forestry|pages=152–163 |location=London |publisher=Routledge |doi=10.4324/9781315627106-11|isbn=978-1-315-62710-6}}</ref> Modeling tools, such as [[i-Tree]], are used by urban foresters to accurately assess the effects of an urban forest's structure; this information is used to quantify ecosystem services and ultimately the economic value of the forest across a variety of locations.<ref name=":05" /> By creating these models, urban foresters are able to quantify and communicate the value of the urban forest to stakeholders and the general public. These evaluations can be used to influence the amount of money allocated to tree management by the government and general populace.<ref name=":34" /> Trees may live a long and healthy life if they continue to receive proper management in the form of maintenance and [[pruning]], which sustains the value of the urban forest.<ref name=":05" /> Moreover, after death, trees have the potential to remain profitable to the community— if utilized correctly.

==== Post life value ====
Typically, wood products such as lumber and wood pellets are associated with rural [[forestry]] and [[logging]]. Annually, urban forestry creates 14.8 metric tons of wood waste in the United States through pruning and removal.<ref name=":15">{{cite web|title=Waste Not, Want Not: Using Urban Wood-Waste to Benefit Communities {{!}} Mississippi State University Extension Service|url=http://extension.msstate.edu/publications/publications/waste-not-want-not-using-urban-wood-waste-benefit-communities|website=extension.msstate.edu|language=en|access-date=2020-04-18|archive-date=2020-08-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200809190650/http://extension.msstate.edu/publications/publications/waste-not-want-not-using-urban-wood-waste-benefit-communities}}</ref> Within urban forestry there are initiatives to use this waste as wood products such as fuel, lumber, art, and more.<ref name=":15" /> These initiatives seek to extend the value of urban trees after their lives.<ref name=":42">{{Cite web|title=Urban Wood Waste: A Guide to Managing Your Community's Resource |url=https://www.ncforestservice.gov/Urban/pdf/NCEX_urban-wood-waste-managing-communitys-resource.pdf |last=Heinen |first=Karla |date=2020|website=NC Forest Service}}</ref> One such initiative is the Virginia Urban Wood Group, a nonprofit with the mission to, "enhance the quality of life through the Stewardship of our Commonwealth's urban and community trees."<ref name=":24">{{Cite web|title=Virginia Urban Wood Group|url=https://treesvirginia.org/outreach/virginia-urban-wood-group|date=2020|website=treesvirginia.org|access-date=2020-04-18}}</ref> The Virginia Urban Wood Group promotes the production and sale of wood products sourced from urban wood waste.<ref name=":24" /> The group connects governmental and commercial professionals such as arborists, municipal foresters, [[Line shaft|mills]], carpenters, and more.<ref name=":24" />

Another group contributing to the urban wood waste industry is Wisconsin Urban Wood. This group collects suitable removed trees from local businesses and arborists and sells the wood to local mills.<ref name=":15" /> While urban [[lumber]] may not be as high of a grade quality as forest grown lumber, these products are suitable for smaller projects such as [[woodwork]]ing and [[artisan]] furniture.<ref name=":24" /> Some localities use their urban lumber to reduce costs on amenity construction— they use their wood to build their [[picnic table]]s and benches.<ref name=":42" /> Additionally, some urban wood initiatives seek the use of [[Reclaimed lumber|reclaimed wood]] to decrease the use of freshly cut lumber.<ref name=":15" />

== Practice ==
[[File:Suburban tree in bag.jpg|thumb|Many trees when first [[Tree planting|planted]] will be placed in a watering bag to help it grow.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Botts|first=Beth|title=Funny-looking green or brown bags help water new trees|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/lifestyles/home-and-garden/ct-home-1010-garden-morton-20190917-hbiqmefh6nc3ff5xbd6kg5q3ae-story.html|access-date=2020-08-08|website=chicagotribune.com|date=17 September 2019 }}</ref>]]

Urban forestry is a [[practical discipline]], which includes [[Tree planting]], [[Tree care|care]], and protection, and the overall management of trees as a collective resource. The urban environment can present many arboricultural challenges such as limited [[root]] and [[Canopy (forest)|canopy]] space, poor [[soil quality]], deficiency or excess of water and light, heat, pollution, mechanical and chemical damage to trees, and mitigation of tree-related hazards. Among those hazards are mostly non-immediate risks like the probability that individual trees will not withstand strong winds (as during a thunderstorm) and damage [[parking]] cars or injure passing [[pedestrian]]s.

Although quite striking in an urban environment, large trees in particular present a continuing dilemma for the field of urban forestry due to the stresses that urban trees undergo from [[automobile exhaust]], constraining hardscape and building foundations, and physical damage (Pickett et al. 2008). Over time these constraints have led urban forestry managers to select smaller statured trees, which is contributing to a shrinking urban forest and less ecosystem services.<ref>{{Cite web |title=International Society of Arboriculture |url=https://wwv.isa-arbor.com/myAccount/login |access-date=2025-10-07 |website=wwv.isa-arbor.com}}</ref> Urban forestry also challenges the arborists that tend the trees. The lack of space requires greater use of [[rigging]] skills and traffic and pedestrian control. The many constraints that the typical urban environment places on trees limits the average lifespan of a city tree to only 32 years – 13 years if planted in a downtown area – which is far short of the 150-year average life span of trees in rural settings (Herwitz 2001).

Management challenges for urban forestry include maintaining a tree and planting site inventory, quantifying and maximizing the benefits of trees, minimizing costs, obtaining and maintaining public support and funding, and establishing laws and policies for trees on public and on private land. Urban forestry presents many social issues that require addressing to allow urban forestry to be seen by the many as an advantage rather than a curse on their environment. Social issues include under funding which leads to inadequate maintenance of urban trees. In the UK the [[National Urban Forestry Unit]] produced a series of case studies around best practice in urban forestry which is archived [http://www.bbcwildlife.org.uk/node/3576 here] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110828100836/http://www.bbcwildlife.org.uk/node/3576 |date=2011-08-28 }}.
[[File:Urban forestry training.jpg|thumb|Proper measurement of diameter at breast height (DBH) as part of an urban forest inventory]]

=== Training and credentials ===
Within the profession and practice of urban forestry, [[training]] and [[credential]]s are often a prerequisite to proper and efficient management. Skills within urban forestry may consist of community-based tree [[stewardship]], [[Restoration ecology|restoration]] of neglected spaces, [[Canopy (biology)|urban canopy]] monitoring and maintenance, and building [[Group cohesiveness|social cohesion]] in urban neighborhoods. Higher education, field experience, and credentials are used to effectively develop and verify these goals. Achievement of the above training can provide prospects for commercial or governmental career opportunities such as a [[Certified Arborist]], Certified [[Forester]], Urban Forester, Professional [[Consultant|Consulting Forester]], Forestry Technician, and many more.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Forester Terms and Definitions. |url=https://ohiodnr.gov/discover-and-learn/safety-conservation/about-ODNR/forestry/landowner-assistance/forester-terms-definitions |website=Ohio Department of Natural Resources.}}</ref>

Higher education in urban forestry is a method of training for aspiring urban foresters. Careers in urban forestry often require higher education that concentrates in urban forestry, [[arboriculture]], [[forestry]], [[horticulture]], [[natural resource management]], [[urban planning]], and [[environmental science]].<ref name=":18">{{Cite journal |last1=Dahle |first1=Gregory A. |last2=Benjamin |first2=Andrew |last3=McGill |first3=David |date=June 2020 |title=Assessment of skills needed in entry-level urban foresters in the USA |journal=Urban Forestry & Urban Greening |language=en |volume=52 |article-number=126694 |doi=10.1016/j.ufug.2020.126694|s2cid=219064340 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2020UFUG...5226694D }}</ref> These [[Interdisciplinarity|interdisciplinary]] educational [[Academic discipline|disciplines]] provide crucial knowledge for urban foresters including collecting attribute data of the urban forest and the implementation of best management practices. Precise data on the urban forest is often scarce and not up-to-date due to the difficulty of traditional sampling approaches.<ref name=":27">{{Cite journal |last1=Tigges |first1=Jan |last2=Lakes |first2=Tobia |date=2017-10-04 |title=High resolution remote sensing for reducing uncertainties in urban forest carbon offset life cycle assessments |journal=Carbon Balance and Management |language=en |volume=12 |issue=1 |page=17 |doi=10.1186/s13021-017-0085-x |issn=1750-0680 |pmc=5628095 |pmid=28980218 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2017CarBM..12...17T }}</ref> Higher education provides insight to modernized technologies that analyze the urban forest, such as remote sensing, and generates accurate data with more precise details on urban [[Canopy (biology)|tree canopy]], individual tree metrics, species, and age structures.<ref name=":27" /> The aforementioned educational training creates a path to becoming a credible urban forester.

While in-classroom education is one method of training, experiential learning is highly recommended in order to hone the more technical aspects of the field, such as tree inventory, planting, and [[Pest control|pest management]].<ref name=":37">{{Cite journal |last1=Scanlan |first1=Caroline |last2=Doroski |first2=Danica |last3=Murphy-Dunning |first3=Colleen |last4=Ashton |first4=Mark |date=2021-01-04 |title=Urban Resources Initiative: A University Model for Clinical Urban Forestry Education |journal=Arboriculture & Urban Forestry |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=34–50 |doi=10.48044/jauf.2021.004 |s2cid=234162944 |issn=1935-5297}}</ref> This field work also extends to training [[social skills]]. Community and client-based relationships often require a certain social expertise to resolve conflict. Through field training and client interaction, skills in conflict management are acquired. This may include, but not limited to effective listening, participatory planning, and leadership.<ref name=":37" /> [[Social engagement]] is increasingly necessary when working with marginalized communities, formatting budget plans, managing aesthetics, and other urban forestry responsibilities. Through [[internship]]s, job experience, and field training opportunities, many skills are developed that are crucial for professions in urban forestry.

Earning credentials and [[certification]]s through professional organizations, such as the International Society of Arboriculture ([[International Society of Arboriculture|ISA]]) and the Tree Care Industry Association (TCIA), are often specific qualifications for becoming an urban forester. The ISA, for example, is a global organization that offers an array of certifications and qualifications, including ISA Certified Arborist.<ref name=":44">{{Cite web |title=ISA Certification and Credentials |url=https://wwv.isa-arbor.com/certification/index |access-date=2022-04-29 |website=International Society of Arboriculture}}</ref> According to a 2020 survey, urban forestry employers desired most employees who possessed the ISA [[Certified Arborist]] credential, followed by a commercial [[pesticide]] applicator license, and a [[commercial driver's license]].<ref name=":18" /> It should be recognized that such credentials require a minimum time period of on-the-job training followed by a written and/or practical exam. To accomplish certifications such as these, online course material and tangible study guides can be purchased, such as through the ISA's website.<ref name=":44" /> After thorough review, computer-based and paper exams can be taken to officially earn a certain credential.<ref name=":44" />

As urban forestry focuses on the extensive management of trees, these organizations are geared to credentialing arborists, or those who manage trees intensively. The TCIA is another professional organization that sets standards for tree firms and provides education and information through publications, conferences, and workshops.<ref name=":53">{{Cite web |title=TCIA Credentialing Programs {{!}} TCIA - Advancing Tree Care Businesses |url=https://www.tcia.org/TCIA/EDUCATION/TCIA_Credentialing_Programs/TCIA/Education_Events/Education/TCIA_Credentialing_Programs/tcia_credentialing_programs.aspx |access-date=2022-04-29 |website=www.tcia.org}}</ref> While the TCIA is designed to provide tree care firms with training and certification, certain programs, such as the Electrical Hazards Awareness Program (EHAP), may benefit those in urban forestry.<ref name=":53" /> An urban forester who directly manages street trees, for example, may find the EHAP useful, for their management decisions because street trees are often affected by overhead and/or underground utilities.

Higher education, field work, and credentials are all methods of training that provide experiences for someone pursuing a career in urban forestry. This training is crucial to establishing trust among urban forest stakeholders and withholding professionalism in the urban forest industry.

=== Street trees ===
[[File:Bz crang main autumn.jpg|thumb|right|Street trees in [[Buzău]], [[Romania]].]]
A street tree is any tree that is growing in a city [[thoroughfare]], whether between the sidewalk and the curb or in an unimproved [[right of way (transit)|right-of-way]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.portlandoregon.gov/trees/article/508002|title=What is a street tree? {{!}} Do I need a permit? {{!}} The City of Portland, Oregon|website=www.portlandoregon.gov|access-date=2020-04-24}}</ref> Street trees provide valuable [[ecosystem service]]s including stormwater mitigation, air pollutant removal, and shade to mitigate the [[urban heat island]] effect. Since street trees are often planted in areas with a high percentage of [[impervious surfaces]], they are an important fraction of an area's overall urban tree cover. When [[Tree planting|planting street trees]], there are many factors to consider and difficulties to overcome. Depending on climate, soil moisture, nutrient dynamic, and location much planning goes into planting street trees. If done incorrectly these trees can cost a municipality time and money to maintain and remove.<ref name=":gala" /> Urban site conditions, Species selection, and tree management are three key aspects of cultivating street trees.

Urban sites present many challenges to street trees because of their adverse conditions. Limited soil volume, high [[Soil compaction (agriculture)|soil compaction]], and intense [[microclimate]]s are common where street trees are planted. Because of these adverse conditions, street trees typically have lower growth rates and lower survival rates than trees planted in nurseries or more natural settings.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sherman |first1=Alex R. |last2=Kane |first2=Brian |last3=Autio |first3=Wesley A. |last4=Harris |first4=J. Roger |last5=Ryan |first5=H. Dennis P. |title=Establishment period of street trees growing in the Boston, MA metropolitan area |journal=Urban Forestry & Urban Greening |date=September 2016 |volume=19 |pages=95–102 |doi=10.1016/J.UFUG.2016.07.006 |bibcode=2016UFUG...19...95S }}</ref> There are also conflicts between tree parts and urban infrastructure because of dense urban environments. Tree roots are known to inflict costly damage by fracturing pavement, which is a common cause for tree removal.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mullaney |first1=Jennifer |last2=Lucke |first2=Terry |last3=Trueman |first3=Stephen J. |title=A review of benefits and challenges in growing street trees in paved urban environments |journal=Landscape and Urban Planning |date=February 2015 |volume=134 |pages=157–166 |doi=10.1016/j.landurbplan.2014.10.013 |bibcode=2015LUrbP.134..157M }}</ref> In order to receive the full benefit of ecosystem services of street trees, urban foresters aim to minimize these conflicts and provide young trees with the highest opportunity to reach maturity.

[[File:Urban Street Tree Melbourne Australia.jpg|thumb|right|alt=Street tree in Melbourne, Australia. Street trees have to survive in often challenging conditions and with numerous human disturbances|Street trees have to be highly tolerant in often hostile conditions and with numerous human disturbances. [[Melbourne]], Australia.]]

A guiding principle of urban forestry is to plant the right tree in the right place. Certain species are more tolerant of adverse urban conditions than others, and urban foresters strive to select species that will maximize benefits and minimize costs for a specific site. For example, yellow-poplar (''[[Liriodendron tulipifera]]'') is known to be intolerant of poor urban soils, and therefore is rarely used as a street tree.<ref name=":dirr">{{cite book|last1=Dirr|first1=Michael|title=The Tree Book|last2=Warren|first2=Keith|publisher=Timber Press, Inc.|year=2019|isbn=978-1-60469-714-8|location=Portland, OR}}</ref> There is no tree species perfectly suited for every site so characteristics of each species are scrutinized to determine their suitability for planting as a street tree. Some important characteristics of street tree species include tolerance of [[Alkali soil|alkaline soils]], compacted soils, low soil volume, de-icing salts, drought, and having good structure. Blackgum (''[[Nyssa sylvatica]]'') and swamp white oak (''[[Quercus bicolor]]'') are species renowned for their adaptability to urban environments, but even they have drawbacks such as Blackgum being difficult to transplant.<ref name=":dirr" /> The London plane (''[[Platanus × hispanica]]'') has been planted in cities all over the world, due to being highly tolerant of urban environments.

Planning is an important step in the establishment of street trees. Policies and guidelines are beneficial in the street tree planning process by lowering costs and improving the health and safety of a municipality. Studies have shown that municipalities that do not abide by policies and guidelines are shown to have higher costs in economic and environmental aspects.<ref name=":gala">{{cite journal |last1=Galenieks |first1=Andrejs |title=Importance of urban street tree policies: A Comparison of neighbouring Southern California cities |journal=Urban Forestry & Urban Greening |date=March 2017 |volume=22 |pages=105–110 |doi=10.1016/j.ufug.2017.02.004 |bibcode=2017UFUG...22..105G }}</ref> Models and formulas may also be used to warrant adequate species diversity for more resiliency to disturbances and stressors.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rogers |first1=Elton C. |last2=Ries |first2=Paul D. |last3=Buckler |first3=Daniel C. |date=2023-09-01 |title=Examining Species Diversity and Urban Forest Resilience in the Milwaukee, Wisconsin (USA) Metropolitan Area |url=https://auf.isa-arbor.com/content/49/5/230 |journal=Arboriculture & Urban Forestry |language=en |volume=49 |issue=5 |pages=230–246 |doi=10.48044/jauf.2023.017 |issn=1935-5297}}</ref> An example of a formula that municipalities abide by in planning is Santamour's 10-20-30 rule.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Santamour |first1=Frank S. |chapter=Trees for Urban Planting: Diversity, Uniformity, and Common Sense |pages=396–422 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SAJQhK1fWDoC&pg=PA396 |editor1-last=Elevitch |editor1-first=Craig R. |title=The Overstory Book: Cultivating Connections with Trees |date=2004 |publisher=PAR |isbn=978-0-9702544-3-6 }}</ref> This formula allows for no more than 10% of the same tree species, no more than 20% of the same genus, and no more than 30% of the same family.

The Species Selection Model focuses on procedures that create a suitable street tree by surveying common species used in urban areas. The Analytic Hierarchy Process is a three layer structure that includes an objective, criteria, and factors. Some factors that may be included in street tree establishment are tree height, DBH, canopy density, and drought resistance. Planning for the physical [[tree planting]] should consider [[bare root]] and balled-and burlapped (B&B) trees. When deciding upon bare root or B&B, species, age, street traffic intensity, site type, wound presence, and dimensions of sidewalk pit cuts should be examined.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jack-Scott |first1=Emily J. |title=Survival and Growth Factors Affecting Community-Planted Urban Street Trees |journal=Cities and the Environment |date=2011 |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=1–16 |doi=10.15365/cate.41102011 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Taking into account bare root and B&B trees along with the above criteria are beneficial in the physical aspects of establishing street trees.

According to the [[Senseable City Lab]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), which measures urban canopy cover in the world's most prominent cities, the city of [[Tampa]] had a Green View Index of 36.1%, representing the total percentage of the city covered by [[street tree|urban trees]]. Tampa was followed by [[Singapore]] (29.3%), [[Oslo]] (28.8%), [[Sydney]] and [[Vancouver]] (both tying at 25.9%), [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]] (25.3%).<ref name=MTI>{{cite web|work=[[The Guardian]]|date=5 November 2019|url=https://www.theguardian.com/cities/2019/nov/05/green-streets-which-city-has-the-most-trees|title=Green streets: which city has the most trees?|access-date=31 October 2020}}</ref> By using satellite data that show trees in parks, homes and on streets, researchers at the [[United States Forest Service]] selected 25 of the most populated urban areas (only one city per country) to analyze how their tree coverage compared, where it put [[New York City]] in first place (with 39.2% of tree cover), followed by [[Moscow]] (29.1%), [[São Paulo]] (27.4%), and [[Paris]] (26.4%).<ref name=MTI/> [[Frankfurt]] was named European City of Trees in 2014 for its care of its trees, and for featuring around 200,000 of trees in public spaces and in [[Frankfurt City Forest]].<ref name=MTI/>

=== Case study: Nashville tree density increase bill ===

In late March 2019, the Nashville Metro Council announced its plan to cut down 21 cherry trees from Riverfront Park so that a temporary outdoor stage could be constructed for the NFL draft.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Gonzalez|first=Tony|date=April 3, 2019|title=Uprooted Cherry Trees In Nashville Spark Protest Against NFL Draft|url=https://www.npr.org/2019/04/03/709573941/uprooted-cherry-trees-in-nashville-spark-protest-against-nfl-draft|access-date=15 October 2021|website=NPR}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Renkl|first=Margaret|date=April 8, 2019|title=The N.F.L.'s Great Cherry Tree Caper|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/04/08/opinion/nfl-nashville-cherry-trees.html|access-date=15 October 2021}}</ref> Immediate public outcry from residents, including a Change.org petition that garnered over 80,000 signatures, pressured the city and the NFL to revise the plan so that only 10 trees would be uprooted and relocated, leaving the remaining ones untouched.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Renkl|first=Margaret|date=September 20, 2021|title=We Need Trees, and Trees Need Us|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/09/20/opinion/city-tree-nature.html|access-date=15 October 2021}}</ref>

Following these events Vice Mayor Jim Shulman contacted the Nashville Tree Conservation Corps, a non-profit that "works to promote, preserve, protect, and plant the tree canopy in Davidson County" in order to prevent future incidents such as this one.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Nashville Tree Conservation Corps|title=About NTCC|url=https://www.nashvilletreeconservationcorps.org/about|access-date=15 October 2021|website=Nashville Tree Conservation Corps}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite web|last=Nashville Tree Conservation Corps|date=August 3, 2021|title=New Protections on Nashville Trees|url=https://www.nashvilletreeconservationcorps.org/treenews/metro-council-considers-stronger-protections-for-public-trees|access-date=15 October 2021|website=Nashville Tree Conservation Corps}}</ref> Thanks to the efforts of the lead sponsor of the bill, council member Jeff Syracuse, and the Nashville Tree Conservation Corps, more than two years later on August 19, 2021, the new public tree bill BL2021-829 was signed into law.

BL2021-829 "seeks to promote transparency and oversight within Metro departments regarding tree removal and replacement."<ref name=":9">{{Cite web|last=Eggers|first=Caroline|date=11 August 2021|title=Nashville Proposes First-Of-Its-Kind Bill To Protect Trees On Public Property|url=https://wpln.org/post/nashville-proposes-first-of-its-kind-bill-to-protect-trees-on-public-property/|access-date=15 October 2021|website=WPLN News - Nashville Public Radio}}</ref> The passage of the bill signaled the Nashville Metro Council's commitment to maintaining [[urban green space]] as the city underwent a development boom. Starting in 2015, Nashville experienced a surge of construction projects that consisted of high rise residential towers to a $220 million office building.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Schneider|first=Keith|date=October 3, 2015|title=Nashville's Skyline Being Reshaped by Building Boom|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/10/14/realestate/commercial/nashvilles-skyline-being-rebuilt-by-building-boom.html|access-date=15 October 2021}}</ref> This development has shown no signs of slowing down, and if left unchecked runs the risk of actively contributing to the [[environmental degradation]] of the city.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Johnston|first=Rhori|date=April 30, 2021|title=Nashville development continues amid pandemic and shows no signs of slowing down|work=NewsChannel 5 Nashville|url=https://www.newschannel5.com/news/nashville-development-continues-amid-pandemic-and-shows-no-signs-of-slowing-down|access-date=15 October 2021}}</ref>

The law specifically addresses the removal of public trees by requiring that the public be notified of their removal at least two weeks beforehand and that replacements are planted.<ref name=":8" /> Key features of the law include the formation of a Tree Working Group, which reviews tree-related policies, and a Tree Review Panel made up of representatives from Water, Parks, Codes, Transportation, General Services, Planning, and the Mayor's Office who oversee public trees. It also mandates that a countywide tree canopy study be conducted every five years in order to keep accurate data on the public trees.<ref name=":9" />

This kind of regulation of the city's trees promises both environmental and social benefits. Maintaining a healthy population of public trees in cities helps to reduce the effect of environmental issues that are common in urban landscapes, such as [[air pollution]] and [[waste heat]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=McDonald|first=Robert|date=October 30, 2016|title=How Urban Trees Can Save Lives|url=https://www.nature.org/en-us/what-we-do/our-insights/perspectives/how-urban-trees-can-save-lives/|access-date=15 October 2021|website=The Nature Conservancy}}</ref> Prioritizing tree growth also supports [[Biophilia hypothesis#Biophilia and conservation|biophilic]] urban design, which has shown to have health benefits and facilitate stronger social and emotional connections among people.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Gehl|first=Jan|title=Outdoor Space and Outdoor Activities|publisher=Routledge|year=2014|isbn=978-0-415-70775-6|location=Abingdon|pages=146–150}}</ref>

== Planning ==
[[File:Parramatta Skyline aerial.png|thumb|Urban canopy of [[Parramatta]], New South Wales, Australia.]]
There are many benefits, costs, and challenges to planning an urban forest. Urban forests provide both ecosystem services and disservices that are considered prior to planning. Urban forests provide services such as improved [[air quality]], [[noise reduction]], temperature mitigation, and [[stormwater]] mitigation when they are placed in the right spot.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Gómez-Baggethun |first1=Erik |last2=Barton |first2=David N. |title=Classifying and valuing ecosystem services for urban planning |journal=Ecological Economics |date=February 2013 |volume=86 |pages=235–245 |doi=10.1016/j.ecolecon.2012.08.019 |bibcode=2013EcoEc..86..235G |hdl=11250/3036001 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Urban forest planning is used to maximize the benefits that trees provide by thoughtfully placing them in the best locations. Challenges that are faced during planning include managing the disservices from trees and valuating their services, the loss/replacement cost of [[green infrastructure]], and the cost of remediating gray infrastructure interference.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Roman |first1=Lara A. |last2=Conway |first2=Tenley M. |last3=Eisenman |first3=Theodore S. |last4=Koeser |first4=Andrew K. |last5=Ordóñez Barona |first5=Camilo |last6=Locke |first6=Dexter H. |last7=Jenerette |first7=G. Darrel |last8=Östberg |first8=Johan |last9=Vogt |first9=Jess |title=Beyond 'trees are good': Disservices, management costs, and tradeoffs in urban forestry |journal=[[Ambio]] |date=2021 |volume=50 |issue=3 |pages=615–630 |doi=10.1007/s13280-020-01396-8|pmid=33011917 |pmc=7882647 |bibcode=2021Ambio..50..615R }}</ref> A major loss of [[green infrastructure]] could alter the sense of place, community identity, and social cohesion of a municipality.<ref name=":0" />

When planning an urban forest there are several practices that can be used. Many municipalities put plans for an urban forest into an official document such as a [[comprehensive planning|master plan]]. While not every city can implement an urban forest plan, it is possible to implement plans for specific areas, such as parks, that would help increase the canopy cover of a [[municipality]].

During the creation of the urban forest management plan, criteria and goals are usually outlined in the plan early in the planning process. Determining criteria is done by assessing the current state of the urban forest and then incorporating criteria for performance goals into the management plan.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |author=W. Andy Kenney |author2=Philip J.E. van Wassenaer |author3=Alexander L. Satel|date=2011|title=Criteria and Indicators for Strategic Urban Forest Planning and Management|url=http://www.fufc.org/soap/kenney_criteria_and_indicators2011.pdf|journal=Arboriculture & Urban Forestry |volume=37 |issue=3 |pages=108–117|doi=10.48044/jauf.2011.015 |s2cid=243929815 }}</ref> Assessment is the first step in planning and provides necessary information on the forest extent, age distribution, [[tree health]], and [[species diversity]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Urban forestry: Planning and managing urban greenspaces|last=Miller, R.W. |author2=Hauer, R.J. |author3=Wener, L.P. |publisher=Waveland Press Inc|year=2015|location=Illinois|pages=11–15}}</ref> Once the assessment is completed, the next step becomes deciding what criteria—or indicators—to incorporate into the plan so that there are set performance goals. Incorporating indicators into the management plan makes it easier to track the progress of the urban forest and whether goals are being met.<ref name=":1" /> Criteria/indicators typically focus on a category of urban forest management and usually include subjects such as:

[[File:Los Angeles (California, USA), South Olive Street -- 2012 -- 5289.jpg|thumb|Green area on South Olive Street in Los Angeles, CA.]]

* The urban forest vegetation and its characteristics such as canopy cover, age distributions, and species diversity.<ref name=":1" />
